A gene is a DNA segment coding for a trait; alleles are alternate forms of that gene. An organism with two identical alleles is homozygous; different alleles make it heterozygous. A Punnett square predicts offspring ratios. For example, crossing two carriers of a recessive condition (Aa × Aa) gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 25% show the recessive phenotype. For two independently assorting genes, multiply individual probabilities: in TtYy × TtYy, the chance of ttYY is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Some traits show incomplete dominance, where heterozygotes display a blended intermediate phenotype, as when red and white snapdragons produce pink offspring. Sex-linked traits ride on the X chromosome, and ABO blood type illustrates codominance plus multiple alleles. Worked example: a pink snapdragon (RW) crossed with pink (RW) yields 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so one-half of the offspring are pink.
key_points: DNA base pairing: A–T and G–C; uracil replaces thymine only in RNA.
Heterozygous × homozygous recessive yields a 1:1 phenotype ratio; heterozygous × heterozygous yields 3:1.
For two independently assorting genes, multiply probabilities (product rule) to get compound genotype ratios.
Incomplete dominance gives a 1:2:1 phenotype ratio in heterozygote crosses.
X-linked recessive traits affect sons of carrier mothers with 50% probability; ABO blood type shows codominance.

items.stem: In a double-stranded DNA molecule, adenine on one strand pairs with which base on the complementary strand?
items.rationale: In double-stranded DNA, complementary base pairing follows Chargaff's rules: adenine always pairs with thymine and guanine always pairs with cytosine. Uracil substitutes for thymine only in RNA.
distractor_rationales: Correct: adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds in double-stranded DNA.
Uracil is the base that pairs with adenine in RNA, not in DNA.
Guanine is a purine like adenine; purines pair with pyrimidines, not with each other.
Cytosine pairs with guanine, not with adenine.

items.stem: A tall pea plant heterozygous for height (Tt) is crossed with a short plant (tt). What fraction of the offspring is expected to be tall?
items.rationale: A Tt × tt cross produces 2 Tt and 2 tt offspring, a 1:1 ratio, so half are tall. The 3:1 ratio would only result from crossing two heterozygotes.
distractor_rationales: 1/4 would apply if the tall parent could only pass a recessive allele, but it can pass T.
Correct: the Punnett square gives Tt and tt, so 1/2 are tall.
3/4 comes from mistakenly using a Tt × Tt cross, which yields a 3:1 ratio.
All tall only occurs if the tall parent were homozygous dominant TT.

items.stem: A pea plant's genotype for flower color is Bb. Which term describes this genotype?
items.rationale: Bb consists of two different alleles for the same gene, which is the definition of a heterozygous genotype. Identical alleles (BB or bb) would make the organism homozygous.
distractor_rationales: Homozygous dominant describes two dominant alleles, BB.
Homozygous recessive describes two recessive alleles, bb.
Correct: two different alleles at the same locus make the organism heterozygous.
Hemizygous describes having only one allele, typical of males for X-linked genes.

items.stem: In a cross between two pea plants heterozygous for both traits (TtYy × TtYy), what is the probability of an offspring with the genotype ttYY?
items.rationale: Assort independently and multiply: P(tt) = 1/4 and P(YY) = 1/4, so P(ttYY) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, one square of the 16-square dihybrid Punnett grid.
distractor_rationales: 9/16 is the fraction of offspring showing both dominant traits (T_ Y_), the classic 9:3:3:1 corner of the square.
3/16 corresponds to ttY_ or T_yy, double-dominant-single-recessive classes.
1/4 is the probability of tt alone, ignoring the YY requirement.
Correct: 1/4 chance of tt times 1/4 chance of YY gives 1/16.

items.stem: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two parents who are both carriers (Aa) have a child. What is the chance that the child is an unaffected carrier?
items.rationale: Aa × Aa yields 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Carriers are the Aa class, so 2 out of 4, or 50%, of the children are unaffected carriers of the recessive allele.
distractor_rationales: Correct: the Punnett square yields 1 AA, 2 Aa, 1 aa, so half are carriers.
25% is the chance of an affected child (aa), not a carrier.
75% counts all unaffected children, mixing carriers with homozygous normal.
100% would require one parent to be homozygous, which carriers are not.

items.stem: In snapdragons, incomplete dominance gives red (RR), white (WW), and pink (RW) flowers. Two pink flowers are crossed. What fraction of their offspring is expected to be pink?
items.rationale: RW × RW yields 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW. Pink flowers are the heterozygous RW class, so 2 of 4, or one-half, of the offspring are expected to be pink.
distractor_rationales: 1/4 is the fraction that are red (RR) or white (WW), not the intermediate phenotype.
Correct: RW appears in two of the four squares, so half the offspring are pink.
3/4 would result if pink were dominant to white, which it is not.
All pink would occur when crossing a red plant with a white plant (RR × WW).

items.stem: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder. A carrier mother (X^H X^h) has children with an unaffected father (X^H Y). What is the probability that a son is affected?
items.rationale: Sons inherit the Y from the father and one X from the carrier mother (X^H X^h). Each son has a 50% chance of receiving X^h and expressing hemophilia, since one X allele is present in males.
distractor_rationales: 0% would be true if the mother were homozygous X^H X^H, but she is a carrier.
25% is the chance that any random child is an affected son, which spreads the probability across both sexes.
Correct: each son has a 50% chance of inheriting the X^h allele from his carrier mother.
100% would require the mother to be homozygous for the recessive allele.

llm_review.issues: Minor wording ambiguity: 25% is the probability of an affected son among all children; for a child known to be a son, the risk is 50%.

items.stem: A father with genotype I^A i (blood type A) and a mother with genotype I^B i (blood type B) have a child. What is the probability the child has blood type O?
items.rationale: Cross I^A i × I^B i yields I^A I^B (AB), I^A i (A), I^B i (B), and ii (O). Only ii produces type O blood, so the probability is 1 of 4.
distractor_rationales: 0% would be true only if neither parent carried the recessive i allele.
1/2 counts the entire offspring classes receiving at least one recessive allele, not just type O.
3/4 is the probability of a child having an antigen (not type O), overcounting the heterozygotes.
Correct: the only genotype yielding type O is ii, which occurs in 1 of 4 squares.

bio_metabolism.title: Cellular respiration and photosynthesis
bio_metabolism.intro_markdown: Cells make ATP from food molecules through cellular respiration, and plants build food molecules through photosynthesis. Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol, producing a small amount of ATP and NADH. If oxygen is present, pyruvate enters the mitochondria, where the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport plus chemiosmosis) extract far more energy. Oxygen's job is to accept electrons at the end of the transport chain, keeping the whole pathway running. If oxygen is absent, fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue, but the ATP yield stays tiny. Photosynthesis runs the energy flow in reverse: light reactions in the thylakoid membranes make ATP and NADPH and release oxygen from water, while the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses that ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. Worked example: glycolysis spends 2 ATP, then produces 4 ATP, so the net gain is 4 − 2 = 2 ATP per glucose.
key_points: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and nets 2 ATP per glucose, regardless of oxygen.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain; fermentation regenerates NAD+ when it is absent.
Light reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and produce ATP, NADPH, and O2; the Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO2 onto RuBP to build sugar.
FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH because it enters the chain at Complex II, bypassing Complex I.
Photosynthesis consumes CO2 and water and releases O2; respiration does the reverse.

items.stem: In eukaryotic cells, glycolysis takes place in which location?
items.rationale: Glycolysis enzymes are free-floating in the cytosol, so it happens outside the mitochondria and requires no oxygen. Only the later stages of aerobic respiration move into the mitochondria.
distractor_rationales: The matrix holds pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle, not glycolysis.
Correct: glycolysis enzymes are soluble and located in the cytosol, so it occurs outside mitochondria.
The inner membrane hosts the electron transport chain, not glycolysis.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, not the breakdown of glucose.

llm_review.issues: Distractors are accurate locations for other pathways (TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, Calvin cycle), making them plausible; option 4 is less parallel since it concerns photosynthesis rather than respiration but remains a legitimate compartment distractor.

items.stem: When a muscle cell temporarily runs out of oxygen, fermentation regenerates NAD+ by converting pyruvate into which product?
items.rationale: Lactic acid fermentation in muscle converts pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making a small amount of ATP when oxygen is scarce.
distractor_rationales: Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products of alcoholic fermentation in yeast, not human muscle.
Acetyl-CoA forms only when oxygen is available and pyruvate enters the mitochondria.
Correct: converting pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep producing ATP.
CO2 and water are products of complete aerobic respiration, not fermentation.

items.stem: The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis occur in which part of the plant cell?
options: The thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast
The cytosol of the plant cell
The inner membrane of the mitochondria
items.rationale: Chlorophyll, photosystems, and the electron transport chain for the light reactions sit in the thylakoid membranes, where light drives ATP and NADPH production and oxygen is released.
distractor_rationales: Correct: photosystems and the electron transport chain of the light reactions are embedded in the thylakoid membranes.
The stroma is where the Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide, not where light is captured.
Light-dependent reactions are membrane events, not free-floating cytosolic reactions.
Mitochondria make ATP by respiration, not by photosynthesis.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the gases exchanged during photosynthesis?
options: Water is produced and oxygen is consumed
Glucose is broken down and carbon dioxide is released
Carbon dioxide is produced and water is consumed
Carbon dioxide is consumed and oxygen is released
items.rationale: The overall equation is 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6 O2. Carbon dioxide and water are consumed; oxygen is released from splitting water.
distractor_rationales: This reverses the water and oxygen roles; water is consumed and oxygen is released.
This describes cellular respiration, the opposite of photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide is a reactant, not a product, of photosynthesis.
Correct: CO2 and water are consumed to build glucose, and O2 is released from splitting water.

llm_review.issues: Stem asks about gases exchanged, but some options include water and glucose; distractors mainly describe cellular respiration or reversed gas exchange. Option 4 is correct.

items.stem: During glycolysis, a cell spends 2 ATP in the energy-investment phase and then produces 4 ATP in the energy-payoff phase. What is the net ATP gain from glycolysis per glucose?
items.rationale: Work it out: the payoff phase makes 4 ATP, and the investment phase spends 2 ATP, so the net gain is 4 − 2 = 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
distractor_rationales: This subtracts the payoff from the investment rather than the reverse; the process makes a small profit.
Correct: 4 ATP produced minus 2 ATP spent gives a net gain of 2 ATP.
This counts the payoff total without subtracting the 2 ATP spent during the investment phase.
This adds the phases (2 + 4 = 6) instead of subtracting the investment from the payoff.

items.stem: Why does aerobic cellular respiration grind to a halt when oxygen is unavailable?
options: Oxygen splits glucose during the investment phase of glycolysis
Oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain
Oxygen directly phosphorylates ADP by substrate-level reactions
Oxygen pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane
items.rationale: Oxygen sits at the end of the electron transport chain, accepting spent electrons and forming water. Without it, NADH cannot be recycled to NAD+, and the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation halt.
distractor_rationales: Glycolysis proceeds without oxygen; it splits glucose using enzymes and 2 ATP, not O2.
Correct: at the chain's end, O2 accepts electrons and combines with H+ to form water, allowing NAD+ and FAD regeneration.
ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis is driven by the proton gradient, not by oxygen acting directly on ADP.
Proton pumping is done by electron transport complexes, not by oxygen itself.

llm_review.issues: Options 1 and 3 are implausible; option 4 is the only strong distractor and conflates ETC proton pumping with oxygen's role as final electron acceptor.

items.stem: In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide is first attached to which molecule?
items.rationale: The enzyme rubisco fixes CO2 onto the 5-carbon acceptor RuBP, producing two 3-phosphoglycerate molecules that ATP and NADPH then convert into sugar.
distractor_rationales: ATP supplies the energy for carbon fixation but does not bind carbon dioxide.
NADPH supplies the electrons for reducing fixed carbon, not the initial binding site.
Glucose is the end product built later from G3P, not the molecule that traps CO2.
Correct: the enzyme rubisco attaches CO2 to RuBP, a 5-carbon sugar, beginning carbon fixation.

items.stem: FADH2 typically produces less ATP per molecule than NADH. What is the reason?
options: Delivers electrons to Complex II, bypassing the proton pumping at Complex I
Carries two electrons while NADH carries four
Cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane
items.rationale: FADH2 donates its electrons to Complex II, skipping Complex I's proton pumps, so it drives less proton-gradient formation and yields about 1.5 ATP versus roughly 2.5 for NADH.
distractor_rationales: Correct: entering at Complex II skips one proton-pumping station, so fewer protons cross the membrane and less ATP is made.
Both carriers donate the same number of electrons; the entry point, not electron count, explains the difference.
FADH2 is made in the citric acid cycle during aerobic respiration, not by fermentation.
The shuttle systems transfer FADH2 electrons into the chain successfully; crossing the membrane is not the limiting issue.

bio_molecules.title: Biological molecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids)
bio_molecules.intro_markdown:
Living things build and run on four classes of large biological molecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Each is assembled from small repeating building blocks (monomers) joined by dehydration synthesis, in which a water molecule is released for every bond formed, and broken apart by hydrolysis, which adds water back.

Carbohydrates (monosaccharides like glucose, C6H12O6) are the cell's fast fuel and structural material. Lipids, including triglycerides (glycerol plus three fatty acids) and phospholipids, are hydrophobic, store dense energy, and build membranes. Proteins are chains of amino acids folded into precise shapes; the shape determines the function, and disrupting that shape (denaturation) disables the protein while leaving its sequence intact. Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) store and transmit hereditary information using nucleotides made of a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogenous base.

Worked example: linking 5 glucose units into a straight chain forms 5 minus 1, or 4 bonds, releasing 4 water molecules.
key_points: Carbohydrates (monosaccharides, formula ratio CH2O) provide quick energy; lipids store energy densely and build membranes.
Proteins are amino-acid polymers whose function depends on shape; denaturation disrupts folding without breaking peptide bonds.
Unsaturated fatty acids contain double-bond kinks and are liquid at room temperature; saturated fats are solid.
Each nucleotide contains a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base; RNA uses ribose and uracil.
Each dehydration-synthesis bond releases one water molecule; a chain of n monomers releases n minus 1 water molecules.

items.stem: Which class of biological molecule serves as the body's most immediate source of cellular fuel?
items.rationale: Carbohydrates, especially simple sugars such as glucose, are metabolized rapidly for ATP, making them the primary quick-energy macromolecule.
distractor_rationales: Correct: carbohydrates, especially simple sugars like glucose, are the body's quickest, most accessible fuel source.
Lipids store more total energy per gram but are broken down slowly, making them long-term rather than quick energy.
Proteins are primarily structural and functional (enzymes, transport), not a preferred quick fuel.
Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information; they are not a usable energy currency.

items.stem: What is the monomer (building block) of proteins?
items.rationale: Proteins are polymers made of amino-acid monomers joined by peptide bonds during dehydration synthesis.
distractor_rationales: Nucleotides are the monomers of nucleic acids, not proteins.
Correct: proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.
Monosaccharides are carbohydrate monomers, such as glucose or fructose.
Fatty acids and glycerol are the building blocks of triglyceride lipids.

items.stem: A triglyceride found in plant oil stays liquid at room temperature. What structural feature of its fatty acid tails explains this?
options: Trans fatty acids with no kinks
Unsaturated fatty acids with double bonds
items.rationale: Double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids create kinks that keep molecules from packing tightly, so these fats remain liquid at room temperature, like olive oil.
distractor_rationales: Saturated fatty acids lack double bonds and stack tightly, remaining solid at room temperature.
Triglycerides with saturated tails, like butter, are solids at room temperature, not liquids.
Correct: cis double bonds create kinks that prevent tight packing, so these fats stay liquid at room temperature.
Trans fats are artificially straightened and behave more like saturated fats, solid or semi-solid at room temperature.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 can also lower melting point, but it is not the characteristic explanation for typical plant oils.

items.stem: Which three components make up a single nucleotide?
options: An amino group, a carboxyl group, and an R group
Glycerol, fatty acids, and a phosphate group
Peptide bonds, a pentose sugar, and helices
A five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base
items.rationale: Every nucleotide, in both DNA and RNA, consists of a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
distractor_rationales: An amino group, carboxyl group, and R group describe an amino acid, the protein monomer.
Glycerol and fatty acids are lipid components; nucleotides contain a pentose sugar, not glycerol.
Peptide bonds, pleated sheets, and helices relate to protein structure, not nucleotide composition.
Correct: every nucleotide has a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.

items.stem: Which structure explains why phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes?
options: A hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails
Three fatty acid tails and no charged head
A glycerol backbone with four phosphate groups
A single polar tail and a nonpolar head
items.rationale: Phospholipids have a polar, water-loving phosphate head and two nonpolar fatty acid tails, so they spontaneously arrange into a bilayer that forms cell membranes.
distractor_rationales: Correct: this amphipathic organization is what forms the bilayer of every cell membrane.
Triglycerides have three nonpolar tails and no phosphate head, so they cannot form a bilayer.
Cholesterol fits within membranes and modulates fluidity but does not self-assemble into bilayers.
Steroid hormones are signaling molecules, not the primary structural unit of membranes.

llm_review.issues: No substantive issue; option 1 correctly describes the amphipathic phospholipid structure. Distractor 3 is implausible, slightly limiting distractor quality.

items.stem: During dehydration synthesis, 12 glucose molecules are joined into one straight-chain polysaccharide. How many water molecules are released?
items.rationale: A linear chain of 12 glucose units has 12 minus 1, or 11, glycosidic bonds. Each bond forms by dehydration synthesis releasing one water molecule, so 11 water molecules are produced.
distractor_rationales: 12 counts the number of glucose monomers, not the number of bonds formed.
10 subtracts two too many; only one fewer bond exists than monomers in a single chain.
6 is half the monomer count, which has no basis in the chemistry.
Correct: 11 glycosidic bonds form, each releasing one water, so 11 water molecules are produced.

llm_review.issues: Correct key is 11. Distractor 12 is plausible, but 10 and 6 are weak.

items.stem: A protein is heated and loses its function, but its amino acid sequence is unchanged. Which bonds were broken?
options: Hydrogen bonds maintaining the folded shape
Covalent bonds in the primary sequence
items.rationale: Denaturation disrupts weak interactions, mainly hydrogen bonds, that hold secondary and tertiary structure, while the covalent primary sequence stays intact.
distractor_rationales: The primary structure is exactly what remains intact; only weak interactions are lost.
Correct: heat disrupts weak hydrogen bonds that maintain secondary and tertiary structure, a change called denaturation.
Peptide bonds are strong covalent bonds defining primary structure; they are not broken by gentle heat denaturation.
Glycosidic bonds link sugars in carbohydrates and are not involved in protein folding.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 is best, but denaturation also disrupts other weak interactions such as ionic and hydrophobic interactions; hydrogen bonds are not the only change.

items.stem: Which statement accurately describes RNA compared with DNA?
options: RNA contains deoxyribose sugar and is always double-stranded
RNA contains thymine in place of uracil
RNA typically is single-stranded, contains ribose, and uses uracil
RNA typically is double-stranded and lacks a phosphate backbone
items.rationale: RNA is usually single-stranded, contains the sugar ribose, and substitutes uracil for the thymine found in DNA.
distractor_rationales: RNA contains ribose, not the deoxyribose sugar found in DNA.
RNA uses uracil in place of thymine; this option reverses the two bases.
Correct: RNA uses ribose sugar and uracil, and is typically single-stranded.
RNA molecules are usually single-stranded, though they can fold on themselves.

bio_scientific_method.title: Scientific method and experimental design
bio_scientific_method.intro_markdown: Science is a process, not just a collection of facts. A researcher starts with an observation, forms a testable hypothesis, designs a controlled experiment, collects data, and draws conclusions that others can verify. In any experiment, the independent variable is the factor the researcher deliberately changes, while the dependent variable is the outcome that is measured. Everything kept constant is a controlled (standardized) variable. A control group receives no treatment or a standard treatment so results can be compared against a baseline. Replication—testing many subjects or repeating trials—reduces the effect of chance and individual variation. Finally, correlation (two things varying together) is not the same as causation; only controlled experiments with random assignment can show that one variable actually causes another. Consider a student who waters identical seedlings with different volumes of water daily and measures plant height after two weeks. Water volume is the independent variable, height is the dependent variable, and light, soil, and temperature are controlled variables. A no-treatment group of seedlings would serve as the control.
key_points: The scientific method moves from observation to testable hypothesis to controlled experiment to analysis and conclusion.
The independent variable is deliberately changed; the dependent variable is the measured outcome.
A control group provides a baseline for comparison by receiving no treatment or standard conditions.
Larger sample sizes and repeated trials reduce the impact of chance and random variation.
Correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other.

items.stem: A student grows identical plants under blue, red, and white light and measures each plant's height after three weeks. In this experiment, the color of light is which variable?
options: The independent variable, because the researcher deliberately changes it
The dependent variable, because it is measured as the outcome
The controlled variable, because it is kept constant in all trials
The control group, because it serves as the baseline for comparison
items.rationale: The researcher intentionally manipulates light color, so it is the independent variable. Growth is the measured dependent variable.
distractor_rationales: Correct. Light color is deliberately manipulated by the experimenter, making it the independent variable.
Plant growth is what is measured in response, so it is the dependent variable, not the manipulated factor.
Controlled variables are held constant, such as water and soil type, not actively changed by the researcher.
A control is a comparison group or condition, not a variable the researcher changes across treatments.

items.stem: Why does a well-designed experiment include a control group?
options: A group that receives every experimental treatment simultaneously
A group that receives no treatment or standard conditions, used as a baseline for comparison
A group that receives the largest dose of the experimental treatment
A group in which the independent variable is allowed to vary freely
items.rationale: The control group is left untreated (or given standard conditions) so any difference between it and the treated groups can be attributed to the treatment itself.
distractor_rationales: Receiving every treatment would confound the results; a control group must be untreated or under standard conditions.
Correct. The control group lacks the experimental treatment, providing a baseline for comparison.
A control group is deliberately not treated so it can show what would happen without the intervention.
A control group does not vary the independent variable; that is the purpose of the experimental groups.

items.stem: Which of the following is a testable scientific hypothesis?
options: Bacteria are the most fascinating organisms on Earth.
All living things should be protected from harm.
Seeds placed in warmer water will sprout faster than seeds in cool water.
Life may exist somewhere beyond our solar system.
items.rationale: A scientific hypothesis predicts a measurable relationship and can be supported or disproven by data. Only the temperature–germination claim meets both criteria.
distractor_rationales: A value judgment about what is interesting cannot be tested by measurement or observation.
An ethical opinion about proper treatment cannot be falsified through data collection.
Correct. This predicts a measurable relationship and can be supported or refuted by data.
A claim about distant planets cannot currently be tested with available methods, so it is speculation rather than a testable hypothesis.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is scientifically investigable in principle, but as worded it is vague and not a testable hypothesis, so option 3 remains best.

items.stem: A researcher applies three different fertilizers to one plant each and concludes that Fertilizer B produces the best growth. What is the main flaw in this experimental design?
options: The experiment is too expensive to be scientifically valid.
The researcher failed to measure the plants with a precise enough ruler.
The experiment lacked a control group of unfertilized plants.
Results from a single plant per group could reflect individual variation rather than the fertilizer's effect.
items.rationale: Using one plant per condition means chance variation between individual plants could explain any observed difference. Replication across many plants is needed to attribute results to the fertilizer.
distractor_rationales: Cost is a practical concern, not the scientific flaw that undermines the conclusion.
Repeating a measurement on one plant improves precision but cannot overcome individual variation across subjects.
The presence of a control group helps, but one plant per group still cannot separate treatment effects from natural variation.
Correct. With one plant per group, differences could reflect individual variation rather than the fertilizer's effect.

items.stem: A survey finds that people who drink herbal tea daily report fewer colds than people who do not. Which conclusion is justified?
options: An observational study cannot establish causation, because other lifestyle factors may explain the difference.
The study must have included thousands of participants before any conclusion can be drawn.
The finding has been repeated enough times to be considered proof of prevention.
Tracking people over a long period automatically eliminates the need for experimental controls.
items.rationale: Tea drinkers may differ in diet, sleep, or stress; such confounding variables could explain fewer colds. Only a controlled experiment with random assignment can demonstrate causation.
distractor_rationales: Correct. Observational studies cannot rule out confounding factors, so controlled experiments are required before claiming causation.
A large sample increases confidence in the correlation but still cannot eliminate confounding variables.
A single study, regardless of design, cannot establish causation without experimental control and replication.
Long-term tracking strengthens the association but still cannot prove a causal mechanism without a controlled experiment.

items.stem: In a clinical trial of a new headache medication, neither the participants nor the researchers evaluating them know who receives the drug and who receives a placebo. What is the purpose of this double-blind design?
options: Double-blinding prevents participants from developing side effects from the medication.
Double-blinding prevents the expectations of both participants and researchers from biasing the results.
Double-blinding allows researchers to identify the drug's chemical composition more accurately.
Double-blinding ensures participants know exactly which treatment they are receiving.
items.rationale: When neither participants nor data collectors know who receives the drug, expectations cannot influence symptom reporting or observation, reducing bias.
distractor_rationales: Blinding does not prevent allergies; it controls psychological and observational bias.
Correct. Blinding keeps expectations of participants and researchers from biasing symptom reports and data recording.
The placebo controls expectations, but double-blinding exists to protect the study's objectivity, not to aid chemical analysis.
The purpose is the opposite: blinding conceals group assignment from both participants and researchers.

items.stem: A student counts the heart rate of water fleas placed in water at 5, 15, and 25 degrees Celsius. The fleas are the same species, kept in identical volumes of water. What is the dependent variable in this experiment?
options: The water temperature, because the student sets it
The volume of water, because it is identical in every trial
The heart rate of the water fleas, because it is the outcome being measured
The species of water flea, because the same organisms are used throughout
items.rationale: The student changes temperature (independent variable) and measures heart rate, making heart rate the dependent variable. Water volume and species are held constant as controlled variables.
distractor_rationales: Water temperature is deliberately manipulated by the student, so it is the independent variable.
Volume is held constant across all trials, making it a controlled variable, not the measured outcome.
Correct. Heart rate is the outcome measured in response to temperature changes, so it is the dependent variable.
Organism choice is kept the same throughout the study, so it is a controlled variable.

items.stem: A researcher tests a new herbicide on two plants and reports a large increase in leaf loss compared with two untreated plants. Which change would most improve the reliability of this finding?
options: Repeating the study with plants of many different species and soil types
Testing only the plants known from prior observation to respond most strongly to the herbicide
Measuring each plant's height with the same ruler for a second time
Testing a large number of plants in each group while keeping all other conditions constant
items.rationale: Testing many plants per group with all other conditions held constant controls for chance and individual variation, which is the best way to increase the reliability of the findings.
distractor_rationales: Changing subjects removes the controlled variables that isolate the cause of the outcome, making results unusable.
Selecting only subjects already sensitive to the herbicide biases the sample and weakens the conclusion.
Repeating the same flawed design replicates the flaw; more precision alone does not fix lack of replication across subjects.
Correct. Testing many plants in each group controls for individual variation and random chance, strengthening the reliability of the findings.

chem_acids_bases.title: Acids, bases, and pH
chem_acids_bases.intro_markdown:
Acids and bases are defined by how they behave in water. An Arrhenius acid donates hydrogen ions (H⁺, carried as hydronium, H₃O⁺), while a base produces hydroxide ions (OH⁻). A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Strong acids and bases, like HCl and NaOH, ionize completely in water; weak ones, like acetic acid, only partly ionize and reach an equilibrium.

pH measures acidity on a log scale: pH = −log[H₃O⁺]. At 25 °C, pure water has pH 7 and [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1×10⁻⁷ M. Each pH unit is a tenfold change, so a move from pH 3 to pH 5 means the hydrogen ion concentration drops by 10×10 = 100-fold. Worked example: if [H₃O⁺] = 1×10⁻⁴ M, then pH = −log(10⁻⁴) = 4.

Buffers, made of a weak acid with its conjugate base, resist pH change. Neutralization follows stoichiometry: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is a 1:1 mole reaction.
key_points: Arrhenius acids donate H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and bases produce OH⁻ in water; Brønsted–Lowry acids donate protons and bases accept them.
pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C, lower is acidic, higher is basic.
Each one-unit change in pH is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
Strong acids/bases ionize completely; weak ones partially ionize and form buffers with their conjugates.
Neutralization requires matching moles: M × V for acid equals (ratio) × M × V for base.

items.stem: According to the Arrhenius definition, which statement best describes a base?
options: It increases the concentration of hydroxide ions in aqueous solution
It increases the concentration of hydrogen ions in aqueous solution
It reacts with an acid to form salt and water only
It removes both hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions from solution
items.rationale: An Arrhenius base is a substance that increases hydroxide ion (OH⁻) concentration when dissolved in water; NaOH is a classic example.
distractor_rationales: Correct: an Arrhenius base raises the hydroxide ion concentration of the solution.
This is the Arrhenius definition of an acid, not a base; the two are opposites.
Neutralization is a reaction acids and bases undergo, not the definition of a base itself.
Both H⁺ and OH⁻ are present in any aqueous solution; this does not define a base and ignores water's constant ion product.

items.stem: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
items.rationale: Pure water at 25 °C has [H₃O⁺] = 1×10⁻⁷ M, so pH = −log(10⁻⁷) = 7, which defines neutrality.
distractor_rationales: Correct: at 25 °C, neutral water has equal 1×10⁻⁷ M H₃O⁺ and OH⁻, giving pH 7.
pH 0 is strongly acidic, not neutral; it corresponds to 1 M acid.
pH 14 is strongly basic, not neutral; it corresponds to 1 M base.
pH 10 is basic; it corresponds to excess hydroxide over hydronium.

items.stem: An aqueous solution has a hydronium ion concentration of 1×10⁻⁴ M. What is its pH?
distractor_rationales: Correct: pH = −log[H₃O⁺] = −log(1×10⁻⁴) = −(−4) = 4.
This inverts the sign of the logarithm, dropping the negative sign in the formula.
The exponent is −4, but the pH is the negative of the log, which is +4.
The hydronium concentration, not the pH, is 1×10⁻⁴ M; this restates the given.

items.stem: Which mixture functions as a buffer in aqueous solution?
options: A solution of a strong acid that fully ionizes in water
A solution created by adding strong base to pure water
A solution that prevents acids and bases from ionizing at all
A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists pH change
items.rationale: A buffer pairs a weak acid with its conjugate base (or weak base with conjugate acid) so added acid or base is consumed, keeping pH nearly constant.
distractor_rationales: This describes a strong acid, which ionizes completely and does not buffer effectively on its own.
Adding strong base to any solution changes pH greatly unless a buffer resists it; buffers work after they exist, not this way.
Buffers work by neutralizing added acid or base via the weak acid/conjugate base pair, not by stopping all ionization.
Correct: the weak acid neutralizes added base and the conjugate base neutralizes added acid, keeping pH nearly constant.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is implausibly absolute; options 1-2 are weak distractors and do not strongly probe common buffer misconceptions.

items.stem: What distinguishes a weak acid from a strong acid in aqueous solution?
options: It reacts with any base in a 1:1 mole ratio regardless of strength
It partially ionizes in water, establishing an equilibrium
It becomes a strong acid once it is dissolved in sufficient water
It produces no hydronium ions when dissolved in water
items.rationale: A weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partially, so an equilibrium forms between intact molecules and ions; a strong acid like HCl ionizes completely.
distractor_rationales: Complete ionization describes a strong acid like HCl, not a weak one.
Correct: weak acids only partially ionize, leaving most molecules intact at equilibrium.
Ionization strength depends on the acid itself, not the water; water does not make weak acids fully ionize.
Weak acids can absolutely raise H₃O⁺ concentration; they just ionize partially rather than completely.

items.stem: A solution's pH rises from 3 to 5. What happens to its hydrogen ion concentration?
options: The hydrogen ion concentration decreases by a factor of 2
The hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 2
The hydrogen ion concentration decreases by a factor of 100
The hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 100
items.rationale: Each pH unit is a tenfold change; two units (3 to 5) means [H₃O⁺] falls by 10² = 100-fold.
distractor_rationales: Subtracting pH units (5 − 3 = 2) does not give the concentration ratio; the scale is logarithmic.
The direction is reversed: raising pH means lowering [H₃O⁺], not raising it.
Correct: pH 3 → 5 is two units, so [H₃O⁺] falls by 10² = 100-fold.
Both the factor and the direction are wrong here.

items.stem: Carbonic acid, H₂CO₃, acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid. What is its conjugate base?
items.rationale: A conjugate base forms when a Brønsted acid donates one proton: H₂CO₃ − H⁺ → HCO₃⁻.
distractor_rationales: Removing two protons gives the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻, which is not the direct conjugate base of H₂CO₃.
This is the conjugate acid of H₂CO₃, formed by adding a proton rather than removing one.
This is the original acid, which still has both acidic protons.
Correct: the conjugate base forms when the acid loses one H⁺, turning H₂CO₃ into HCO₃⁻.

items.stem: What volume of 0.50 M NaOH is required to completely neutralize 25 mL of 0.40 M HCl? (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O)
items.rationale: Moles HCl = 0.025 L × 0.40 M = 0.010 mol. The 1:1 reaction needs 0.010 mol NaOH; volume = 0.010 ÷ 0.50 M = 0.020 L = 20 mL.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 0.025 L × 0.40 mol/L = 0.010 mol HCl; at 1:1 stoichiometry, 0.010 ÷ 0.50 M = 0.020 L = 20 mL.
This assumes equal volumes are needed, ignoring that the concentrations differ.
This uses an inverted ratio of molarities (0.40/0.50 inverted), giving 16 mL.
This assumes 0.625 mol of NaOH per mol of HCl, which is not the stoichiometry.

chem_atoms.title: Atomic structure, isotopes, and ions
chem_atoms.intro_markdown: Every atom has a dense nucleus made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. The atomic number equals the number of protons, and it alone fixes an element's identity: any atom with 17 protons is chlorine, no matter what else is true about it. The mass number is the total count of protons plus neutrons in one nucleus. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same protons) with different neutron counts, so they have different mass numbers — carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but carbon-12 has 6 neutrons while carbon-14 has 8. Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, giving a positive cation; gaining electrons gives a negative anion. Worked example: sodium (atomic number 11) loses one electron, leaving 11 protons and 10 electrons, so it carries a 1+ charge. Protons and neutrons almost never change during ordinary chemistry.
key_points: Atomic number = number of protons; it defines which element an atom is.
Mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Isotopes share the same number of protons but differ in neutrons (and mass number).
Electrons equal protons in a neutral atom; charge = protons − electrons.
Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of isotope masses, not a simple average.

items.stem: An atom is found to contain exactly 17 protons. Which element is it?
items.rationale: The number of protons is the atomic number and defines the element. Atomic number 17 belongs to chlorine, so any atom with 17 protons is chlorine regardless of neutrons or electrons.
distractor_rationales: Chlorine is correct because the number of protons (17) is the atomic number, and the element with atomic number 17 is chlorine.
Argon is element 18; choosing it comes from matching a nearby mass number instead of counting protons.
Sulfur is element 16; this reflects an off-by-one error in reading the periodic table.
Potassium is element 19; this mistakes the next element's atomic number for this one.

items.stem: Carbon-14 is an isotope of carbon, which has an atomic number of 6. How many neutrons are in the nucleus of carbon-14?
items.rationale: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 14 − 6 = 8. Carbon's identity comes from its 6 protons.
distractor_rationales: 6 counts only the protons, forgetting that neutrons add to the mass number.
8 is correct: 14 minus 6 protons leaves 8 neutrons.
14 is the mass number, mistakenly used directly as the neutron count.
20 results from adding the mass number and the atomic number instead of subtracting.

items.stem: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element?
options: A sodium atom and a sodium ion
items.rationale: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons. Hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2 both have 1 proton but differ in neutrons, fitting the definition.
distractor_rationales: Carbon-12 and nitrogen-14 have similar mass numbers but different proton counts, so they are different elements, not isotopes.
A sodium atom and its ion differ in electrons, not in neutrons; isotopes must differ in neutron number.
Hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2 both have 1 proton but 0 and 1 neutrons respectively, so they are isotopes.
Potassium-39 and calcium-40 are different elements with different proton counts; similar mass numbers do not make isotopes.

items.stem: Magnesium has an atomic number of 12. How many electrons does a magnesium ion with a 2+ charge (Mg2+) contain?
items.rationale: Neutral magnesium has 12 electrons (equal to its 12 protons). A 2+ cation lost 2 electrons, leaving 12 − 2 = 10 electrons; the proton count stays 12.
distractor_rationales: 10 is correct: neutral magnesium has 12 electrons, and losing 2 for the 2+ charge leaves 10.
12 is the electron count of a neutral magnesium atom, ignoring the ion's lost electrons.
14 results from wrongly adding 2 electrons instead of removing them.
8 mistakenly subtracts 2 twice or confuses magnesium with an element of atomic number 10.

items.stem: A sulfur atom (atomic number 16, mass number 34) gains two electrons to form the sulfide ion. How many electrons does this ion contain?
items.rationale: Sulfur starts with 16 electrons when neutral. Gaining 2 electrons gives the 2− charge, so the ion has 16 + 2 = 18 electrons while protons remain 16.
distractor_rationales: 16 is the proton count of neutral sulfur, not the electron count of the 2− ion.
34 is the mass number, which counts protons plus neutrons, not electrons.
2 is the charge magnitude, mistakenly used as the electron count.
18 is correct: 16 electrons plus 2 gained equals 18, one more than the 17 protons.

items.stem: An element has two naturally occurring isotopes: 90% of atoms have a mass of 20 amu and 10% have a mass of 22 amu. What is the element's average atomic mass?
items.rationale: Multiply each isotope's mass by its fractional abundance and add: (0.90)(20) + (0.10)(22) = 18.0 + 2.2 = 20.2 amu. The average sits near 20 because that isotope dominates.
distractor_rationales: 21.0 comes from taking a plain unweighted average of 20 and 22, ignoring the different abundances.
22.0 simply reports the mass of the heavier isotope, ignoring abundance weighting.
20.0 assumes the heavier isotope does not exist, using only the light isotope's mass.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the phosphide ion ³¹P³⁻ (phosphorus, atomic number 15)?
items.rationale: Phosphorus has atomic number 15, so it has 15 protons. A 3− charge means it gained 3 electrons: 15 + 3 = 18 electrons. Neutrons (16 here) do not affect charge.
distractor_rationales: This reverses the ion's charge; 15 protons with 18 electrons is the actual arrangement.
18 protons would make the atom argon, not phosphorus; the neutron count was confused with protons.
12 protons would make the atom magnesium, not phosphorus; the electron count was confused with protons.
This is correct: 15 protons identify phosphorus, and gaining 3 electrons gives 18 electrons.

items.stem: An ion is found to contain 26 protons and 23 electrons. What is the identity and charge of this ion?
options: A cobalt ion with a 3+ charge
An iron ion with a 3− charge
An iron ion with a 3+ charge
A manganese ion with a 3+ charge
items.rationale: With 26 protons the atom is iron (atomic number 26). Three more protons than electrons (26 vs 23) means 3 electrons were lost, producing a charge of 3+.
distractor_rationales: Cobalt has 27 protons, so 26 protons cannot belong to cobalt.
The ion has more protons than electrons, which gives a positive, not negative, charge.
This is correct: 26 protons identify iron, and 26 − 23 = 3 missing electrons gives a 3+ charge.
Manganese has 25 protons, so it does not match an atom with 26 protons.

chem_bonding.title: Ionic, covalent, and hydrogen bonds
chem_bonding.intro_markdown: Atoms bond three main ways. In an ionic bond, one atom transfers electrons to another, creating oppositely charged ions (like Na+ and Cl−) that attract each other. In a covalent bond, two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; if the sharing is uneven (as between H and O in water), the bond is polar covalent. A hydrogen bond is weaker: it occurs between a hydrogen atom attached to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another N, O, or F atom. Worked example: in water, each O–H link is a polar covalent bond, but the attraction between the slightly positive H of one molecule and the lone pair on the O of a neighboring molecule is a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonds explain water's high boiling point and its surface tension, while ionic bonds explain why salts like NaCl have high melting points and conduct electricity only when dissolved or molten.
key_points: Ionic bonds transfer electrons between metal and nonmetal atoms; covalent bonds share them; hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules.
Hydrogen bonds require hydrogen attached to N, O, or F interacting with a lone pair on another N, O, or F.
Water's high boiling point and surface tension come from hydrogen bonds between molecules, not from breaking O–H covalent bonds.
Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved or molten because their ions are free to move; covalent molecular solutes like sugar do not conduct.
Formula writing for ionic compounds follows charge balance: the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge.

items.stem: Which statement best describes how an ionic bond forms between sodium and chlorine?
options: A bond formed when one atom completely transfers electrons to another
A bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons
A bond formed by a sea of mobile electrons around metal ions
A weak attraction between a hydrogen atom and a nearby electronegative atom
items.rationale: Ionic bonding is the complete transfer of valence electrons from a metal to a nonmetal, producing oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction, as in NaCl.
distractor_rationales: Correct: ionic bonding is defined by complete transfer of valence electrons, producing oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.
This describes covalent bonding, where electrons are shared between nuclei rather than transferred.
This describes metallic bonding, where delocalized electrons move through a lattice of positive metal ions.
Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules and involve no transfer of electrons.

items.stem: The O–H bond within a single water molecule is classified as which type of bond?
options: Ionic, because oxygen is a metal-like acceptor
Polar covalent, because the electrons are shared unequally
Nonpolar covalent, because the electrons are shared equally
Hydrogen, because the bond contains hydrogen
items.rationale: Oxygen (3.5) and hydrogen (2.2) differ by about 1.3 in electronegativity, so electrons are shared unevenly but not transferred; each O–H bond is polar covalent.
distractor_rationales: Electrons are shared in this bond, not transferred, so it is not ionic.
Correct: the 1.4 difference in electronegativity produces unequal sharing within a covalent bond, making it polar covalent.
Sharing is unequal because of the electronegativity difference, so nonpolar covalent is incorrect.
A hydrogen bond exists between separate water molecules, not within the O–H bond itself.

llm_review.issues: Option 1 uses imprecise wording ('metal-like acceptor'), but the key and rationale are correct.

items.stem: Water boils at 100 °C, much higher than other molecules of similar mass. What accounts for this unusually high boiling point?
options: Ionic bonds within each water molecule
Covalent bonds being unusually weak in water
Hydrogen bonds between neighboring water molecules
London dispersion forces between hydrogen atoms
items.rationale: Boiling requires separating molecules, not breaking O–H covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules are strong intermolecular attractions, so water boils far above similar-sized nonpolar molecules.
distractor_rationales: Ionic bonds within the molecule would require electron transfer; hydrogen and oxygen instead share electrons.
Covalent O–H bonds exist within each molecule and are far stronger than the attractions responsible for boiling point elevation.
Correct: hydrogen bonds between water molecules require extra energy to break, giving water its unusually high boiling point.
London dispersion forces are weak temporary attractions significant in nonpolar molecules, not the main force in water.

llm_review.issues: Boiling point of 100 °C applies at 1 atm; minor omission of pressure but does not affect the correct answer.

items.stem: How many total valence electrons must be accounted for when drawing the Lewis structure of CO2?
items.rationale: Carbon contributes 4 valence electrons and each oxygen contributes 6, so 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 valence electrons, enough for two double bonds and two lone pairs per oxygen in O=C=O.
distractor_rationales: This counts only the eight electrons actually shared in the two double bonds, not all valence electrons.
This total omits carbon's four valence electrons, counting only the two oxygens.
This total treats carbon as if it had only two valence electrons instead of four.
Correct: 4 from carbon plus 6 from each of two oxygens gives 16 valence electrons to place in the structure.

items.stem: Sodium forms a +1 ion and oxygen forms a −2 ion. What is the correct formula of the ionic compound they form together?
items.rationale: Sodium loses one electron to become Na+, while oxygen gains two electrons to become O2−. Charge neutrality requires two Na+ for every O2−, giving the formula Na2O.
distractor_rationales: One sodium atom supplies only one electron, but oxygen needs two to complete its octet, so this ratio leaves oxygen short.
Correct: each sodium gives up one electron, so two sodium atoms are needed to supply the two electrons oxygen requires.
Two sodium atoms would donate only two electrons total; three would donate three, which exceeds what neutral oxygen can accept.
This reverses the ions' roles; oxygen is the electron acceptor, not sodium, and formulas reflect the charges after transfer.

llm_review.issues: Distractors are usable, though option 4 mainly tests cation-first formula convention rather than ionic ratio.

items.stem: Ammonia (NH3) molecules contain N–H bonds and also attract each other across molecules. Which pair of bond types describes these two situations?
options: Covalent bonds within the molecule and ionic bonds between molecules
Covalent bonds within the molecule and hydrogen bonds between molecules
Hydrogen bonds within the molecule and ionic bonds between molecules
items.rationale: Within NH3, nitrogen and hydrogen share electrons in polar covalent N–H bonds. Between molecules, each N–H hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on nitrogen of a neighboring NH3, forming hydrogen bonds.
distractor_rationales: An ionic compound of nitrogen and hydrogen would require electron transfer, but these two nonmetals share electrons instead.
N–H bonds are polar covalent, not ionic, because nitrogen and hydrogen are both nonmetals that share electrons.
Correct: covalent N–H bonds hold each molecule together, while hydrogen bonds attract one NH3 molecule to its neighbors.
The forces between molecules are hydrogen bonds, not ionic attractions, since no full charges are present.

items.stem: Which solute, when dissolved in pure water, would produce a solution that conducts electricity well?
items.rationale: NaCl dissociates into mobile Na+ and Cl− ions in water, making the solution conductive. Covalent solutes like sugars and alcohol dissolve as neutral molecules, so their solutions do not conduct.
distractor_rationales: Correct: NaCl is ionic and dissociates into Na+ and Cl− ions that carry current through the solution.
Glucose is a covalent molecular compound that dissolves as neutral molecules, so no ions are present to carry charge.
Ethanol dissolves as intact neutral molecules and produces no ions, so the solution does not conduct.
Sucrose is covalent and dissolves as whole neutral molecules, giving a nonconducting solution.

items.stem: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) boils at 19.5 °C, while the other hydrogen halides boil lower despite being heavier. Which compound shows the highest boiling point, and why?
items.rationale: HF is the only hydrogen halide with hydrogen bonded to fluorine, allowing strong hydrogen bonding between molecules; this raises its boiling point above the heavier HCl, HBr, and HI, which rely only on weaker dispersion forces.
distractor_rationales: HCl lacks hydrogen bonding because chlorine is not one of N, O, or F; its polarity alone is weaker than HF's hydrogen bonding.
HBr is larger and more polarizable, but its dispersion forces still do not exceed the hydrogen bonding in HF.
HI is the heaviest and has the strongest dispersion forces, yet these remain weaker than hydrogen bonds, so it boils below HF.
Correct: only HF has hydrogen bonded to fluorine, giving strong hydrogen bonding that yields the highest boiling point of the group.

chem_moles_solutions.title: Moles, molarity, and solutions
chem_moles_solutions.intro_markdown: A mole is a counting unit: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its molar mass from the periodic table. Moles connect grams to particles, and they are the currency of solutions. Molarity (M) is defined as moles of solute per liter of solution (not per liter of solvent). To find moles from mass, divide grams by molar mass. To find molarity, divide moles by liters: M = n ÷ V. Dilutions follow M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, where V₂ is the total final volume, so water added equals V₂ − V₁. When an ionic solid dissolves, each ion's concentration scales with its subscript. Worked example: 29.2 g NaCl (MM = 58.44 g/mol) is 0.500 mol; dissolved to a final volume of 0.250 L, it gives M = 0.500 ÷ 0.250 = 2.00 M. Watch units at every step: milliliters must become liters before dividing.
key_points: Molarity (M) = moles of solute per liter of solution; convert mL to L before dividing.
Moles from mass: n = grams ÷ molar mass; mass from moles: m = n × molar mass.
Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂; V₂ is the total final volume, so water added = V₂ − V₁.
Ionic compounds dissociate: the concentration of each ion equals its subscript times the formula-unit molarity.
When mixing solutions, add the moles from each part and divide by the total combined volume.

items.stem: Which statement best defines the molarity (M) of a solution?
options: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Moles of solute per liter of solution
Grams of solute per liter of solution
Moles of solute per liter of pure solvent
items.rationale: Molarity is defined as moles of solute per liter of total solution. Moles per kilogram of solvent is molality; grams per liter is mass concentration.
distractor_rationales: This describes molality (moles per kilogram of solvent), a different unit typically used for colligative properties.
Correct. Molarity is moles of solute divided by liters of final solution.
This gives a mass concentration (g/L), not moles per liter, so it does not count particles.
Molarity is defined per liter of solution; the solvent alone ignores the volume the solute contributes.

items.stem: How many moles of NaCl are present in 29.2 g of NaCl (molar mass 58.44 g/mol)?
items.rationale: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 29.2 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol = 0.500 mol of NaCl.
distractor_rationales: Correct. Dividing mass by molar mass gives 29.2 ÷ 58.44 = 0.500 mol.
This results from inverting the division (58.44 ÷ 29.2), placing molar mass over grams.
This results from doubling the molar mass before dividing.
This treats the gram amount as if it were already a count in moles.

llm_review.issues: 29.2 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol = 0.4997 mol, which rounds to 0.500 mol. Key is correct.

items.stem: A student dissolves 0.75 mol of KCl in enough water to make 250 mL of solution. What is the molarity?
items.rationale: Convert first: 250 mL = 0.250 L. Molarity = 0.75 mol ÷ 0.250 L = 3.0 M.
distractor_rationales: This comes from multiplying moles by liters (0.75 × 0.25) instead of dividing.
This comes from dividing by 250 instead of 0.250, leaving milliliters unconverted.
Correct. Converting 250 mL to 0.250 L and dividing gives 0.75 ÷ 0.250 = 3.0 M.
This assumes one mole per liter regardless of the volume actually prepared.

items.stem: What mass of glucose (molar mass 180 g/mol) is needed to prepare 500 mL of a 0.10 M solution?
items.rationale: Moles needed = 0.10 mol/L × 0.500 L = 0.050 mol; mass = 0.050 mol × 180 g/mol = 9.0 g.
distractor_rationales: This comes from using 1.0 L instead of 0.500 L, doubling the moles of glucose.
This comes from using 0.010 mol instead of 0.050 mol, a misplaced decimal in the volume.
This comes from using 500 mL as 500 L worth of moles (0.5 mol) instead of 0.050 mol.
Correct. 0.050 mol × 180 g/mol = 9.0 g of glucose.

items.stem: A lab technician needs 250 mL of 1.5 M HCl from a 12 M stock solution. What volume of stock should be measured out?
items.rationale: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, so V₁ = (1.5 M × 250 mL) ÷ 12 M = 31.25 mL, rounded to 31 mL of stock.
distractor_rationales: Correct. V₁ = M₂V₂ ÷ M₁ = (1.5 × 250 mL) ÷ 12 = 31 mL, then diluted to the mark.
This comes from inverting the dilution equation (M₁V₁ ÷ M₂), which cannot exceed the final volume.
This comes from treating the target as 0.15 M, a decimal-place error in M₂.
This comes from using 6.0 M as the stock concentration instead of 12 M.

items.stem: What is the chloride ion concentration in a 0.40 M aqueous solution of AlCl₃, assuming complete dissociation?
items.rationale: AlCl₃ dissociates completely: each formula unit gives 3 Cl⁻, so [Cl⁻] = 3 × 0.40 M = 1.2 M.
distractor_rationales: This reports the formula-unit concentration and ignores the three chloride ions released.
Correct. Each formula unit releases 3 Cl⁻ ions, so 3 × 0.40 M = 1.2 M.
This comes from dividing by 3 instead of multiplying by 3.
This comes from multiplying by 2, using the charge or a wrong subscript.

items.stem: 50 mL of 0.20 M NaCl is mixed with 150 mL of 0.10 M NaCl. Assuming volumes are additive, what is the final NaCl concentration?
distractor_rationales: This comes from simply averaging the two molarities, (0.20 + 0.10) ÷ 2, ignoring the unequal volumes.
This reports the total moles (0.025 mol) as if it were a concentration.
This comes from adding the two molarities, ignoring dilution by the combined volume.
Correct. Total moles 0.025 ÷ total volume 0.200 L = 0.125 M.

items.stem: A solution is prepared by diluting 100 mL of 5.0 M reagent to a final concentration of 2.0 M. Assuming volumes are additive, how much water must be added?
items.rationale: V₂ = M₁V₁ ÷ M₂ = (5.0 M × 100 mL) ÷ 2.0 M = 250 mL total. Water added = 250 − 100 = 150 mL.
distractor_rationales: This is the final total volume V₂; the question asks only for the water added, so the stock volume must be subtracted.
This comes from inverting the equation to V₁ = M₂V₁ ÷ M₁, swapping which concentration divides.
Correct. V₂ = (5.0 × 100) ÷ 2.0 = 250 mL, so water added = 250 − 100 = 150 mL.
This comes from computing 100 × (5.0 − 2.0) ÷ 5.0, using only the change in concentration fraction.

chem_periodic_table.title: Periodic table trends and groups
chem_periodic_table.intro_markdown: The periodic table is arranged so that several properties change smoothly with position. Across a period (left to right), protons are added to the nucleus while electrons enter the same shell, so effective nuclear pull on the outer electrons grows: atomic radius shrinks, ionization energy rises, and electronegativity rises. Down a group, each element adds a new outer shell, so radius grows and ionization energy falls, even though nuclear charge also grows. Ions add a wrinkle: cations are smaller than their parent atoms (fewer electrons, often no outer shell), while anions are larger (added electron–electron repulsion). Ions with the same electron count (an isoelectronic series, e.g., O2−, F−, Na+, Mg2+) shrink as proton count rises, because more nuclear charge pulls the same cloud tighter. Worked example: comparing Cl (about 99 pm) with Cl− (about 181 pm), the anion is larger because the extra electron expands the 3p cloud through repulsion.
key_points: Atomic radius decreases left to right across a period (same shell, more protons) and increases down a group (new outer shell).
First ionization energy and electronegativity increase across a period and decrease down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger, due to changed electron–electron repulsion.
In an isoelectronic series, more protons mean a smaller ion: O2− > F− > Na+ > Mg2+.
Know the exceptions: Al's first ionization energy is below Mg's because Al removes a higher-energy 3p electron; noble gases are inert because their valence shells are full.

items.stem: Moving from left to right across period 3, from sodium (Na) to chlorine (Cl), what happens to atomic radius?
options: It decreases, because increasing nuclear charge pulls the same outer shell in more tightly
It increases, because each element gains more electrons than protons
It stays essentially constant, because electrons enter the same principal shell
It first increases, then decreases, peaking at the middle of the period
items.rationale: Across a period the valence electrons occupy the same shell while protons increase, so effective nuclear charge rises and the shell contracts; radius decreases from Na to Cl.
distractor_rationales: Correct: Zeff rises across the period, contracting the same-n valence shell, so radius steadily decreases.
This reverses the trend; radius increases going down a group, not across a period.
Radius does change measurably across every period, from alkali metals to halogens.
Radius decreases monotonically; there is no mid-period peak in radius.

items.stem: Going down group 17 from fluorine to iodine, how does the first ionization energy change, and why?
options: It increases, because each element has more protons attracting its outer electron
It decreases, because the outer electron sits in a higher, more shielded shell farther from the nucleus
It stays constant, because halogens all have seven valence electrons
It alternates up and down unpredictably within the group
items.rationale: Down a group, the valence electron occupies a shell farther from the nucleus and is shielded by inner electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it.
distractor_rationales: Down a group ionization energy falls, not rises, because the valence electron is farther out.
Correct: distance and shielding outweigh added protons, so F is hardest and I easiest to ionize in group 17.
There is a clear, monotonic decrease down every group.
No zigzag occurs within a single group for this property.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is implausible as a distractor; the other distractors represent common misconceptions.

items.stem: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
items.rationale: Electronegativity rises across a period and up a group, so the element at the top right (excluding noble gases) wins: fluorine, at about 3.98, is the most electronegative element.
distractor_rationales: Oxygen is highly electronegative (3.44) but ranks third, below fluorine.
Chlorine's electronegativity (3.16) is close but below fluorine's 3.98.
Correct: fluorine, at about 3.98 on the Pauling scale, has the highest electronegativity of any element.
Nitrogen (3.04) is well below oxygen, chlorine, and fluorine in electronegativity.

items.stem: How does the radius of a chloride ion (Cl−) compare with that of a neutral chlorine atom?
options: Cl− is smaller, because its extra electron is pulled in more tightly by the 17 protons
Cl− is smaller, because forming an anion always compresses the electron cloud
Cl− is exactly the same size, since the added electron enters the existing 3p subshell
Cl− is larger, because the added electron increases repulsion within the 3p subshell, expanding the cloud
items.rationale: Gaining an electron adds negative charge but no protons, so electron–electron repulsion expands the cloud; the chloride ion (about 181 pm) is far larger than neutral chlorine (about 99 pm).
distractor_rationales: Extra electrons add repulsion rather than extra nuclear pull; the anion expands.
Anions essentially always expand relative to the neutral atom.
Added charge does change size: the 3p cloud expands, roughly doubling the covalent radius.
Correct: added electron–electron repulsion in the 3p subshell expands the cloud, so Cl− is much larger.

llm_review.issues: Neutral chlorine radius depends on the radius definition used, but Cl− is still larger.

items.stem: Which period-3 element has the smallest atomic radius: sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), aluminum (Al), or silicon (Si)?
items.rationale: All four are in period 3 with valence electrons in the same shell; silicon has the most protons (14), the highest effective nuclear charge, and therefore the smallest atomic radius.
distractor_rationales: Correct: silicon lies farthest right, so it has the greatest effective nuclear charge and the smallest radius of the four.
Sodium is farthest left and has the largest radius of the set.
Magnesium is larger than aluminum and silicon; it is not the smallest.
Aluminum is larger than silicon because its 13 protons pull less strongly than silicon's 14.

items.stem: Although ionization energy generally increases left to right across a period, aluminum's first ionization energy is lower than magnesium's. Which statement explains this?
options: Al has a higher first ionization energy, because it lies to the right of Mg and periodic trends never have exceptions
Mg has a higher first ionization energy, because Al's outermost electron is in a higher-energy 3p orbital and is easier to remove than Mg's 3s electron
They have identical first ionization energies, since both are period-3 metals with two outer electrons involved
Al has a higher first ionization energy, because its 13 protons attract the outer electron more strongly than Mg's 12 protons
items.rationale: This is a known exception: Al's outermost electron is in 3p, higher in energy and more shielded than Mg's filled 3s electrons, so aluminum's first ionization energy is lower.
distractor_rationales: Simply reading left to right fails here: aluminum's 3p electron is the anomaly.
Correct: the subshell change makes aluminum's 3p electron easier to remove, so its ionization energy is lower.
They differ measurably; the anomaly is a classic exception to the period trend.
The proton count is real, but the higher-energy 3p electron still comes off more easily than magnesium's 3s electron.

items.stem: The ions O2−, F−, Na+, and Mg2+ all contain 10 electrons. Which ion has the largest radius?
items.rationale: All four ions hold 10 electrons (isoelectronic). Radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, so the ion with the fewest protons—oxide, O2− with 8—is the largest.
distractor_rationales: With equal electrons, the most protons (Mg2+, 12) give the smallest ion, not the largest.
Na+ has 11 protons, so it is larger than Mg2+ but smaller than both anions.
Correct: fewest protons pulling the same 10-electron cloud means the largest radius.
F− with 9 protons is larger than Mg2+ and Na+ but smaller than O2− with 8 protons.

items.stem: Why are the group 18 noble gases chemically unreactive compared with neighboring elements?
options: They have the highest ionization energies of all elements in every period
They have no valence electrons at all
They are the largest atoms in their periods, so they cannot bond
Their valence s and p subshells are completely filled, so they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons
items.rationale: Noble gases possess filled outer shells (ns2np6, or 1s2 for helium), a stable configuration requiring large energy changes to alter; hence their famous chemical inertness.
distractor_rationales: Helium's is the highest, but group 18 ionization energies drop sharply down the group; that is not the general explanation.
Noble gases have full valence shells, not empty ones.
Noble gases are actually relatively small atoms because their shells are tightly held.
Correct: filled valence shells mean virtually no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons, so noble gases are chemically inert.

chem_reactions.title: Balancing equations and reaction types
chem_reactions.intro_markdown: Balancing chemical equations rests on one rule: atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so every element must appear in equal numbers on both sides of the arrow. You change only coefficients (the numbers in front of formulas), never subscripts. Worked example: methane burns as CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. Carbon balances at one, then hydrogen: four H atoms on the left require 2H2O on the right. That gives four O atoms on the right, so oxygen needs 2O2. The balanced equation is CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Reactions also fall into patterns worth recognizing at a glance: combination (two reactants form one product), decomposition (one reactant forms several products), single replacement (one element swaps in for another), double replacement (two compounds trade partners, often forming a precipitate), and combustion (a fuel reacting with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water).
key_points: Atoms are conserved: adjust coefficients only, never subscripts
Treat polyatomic ions (like SO4 2-) as whole units when they appear unchanged on both sides
Balance oxygen and hydrogen last, especially in combustion reactions
Recognize the five types: combination, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion
Hydrocarbon combustion always produces CO2 and H2O

items.stem: Which reaction type is shown by 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl?
items.rationale: Two elements join to build a single product, sodium chloride. Forming one product from multiple reactants defines a combination (synthesis) reaction.
distractor_rationales: Two separate reactants (Na and Cl2) join to form a single product (NaCl), the defining pattern of a combination or synthesis reaction.
Decomposition runs the opposite direction: one reactant splits into two or more products, as in one compound breaking apart.
Single replacement requires a free element taking the place of another element inside a compound; both reactants here are elements.
Double replacement requires two compounds exchanging partners; no compounds appear among the reactants.

items.stem: When methane burns according to CH4 + ___ O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, what coefficient fills the blank?
items.rationale: Balance carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen last: 2H2O carries 4 H atoms, and the right side then has 2 + 2 = 4 O atoms. Two O2 molecules supply exactly 4 O atoms.
distractor_rationales: One O2 supplies only 2 oxygen atoms, but the products hold 4.
The products contain 2 oxygen atoms in CO2 plus 2 in 2H2O, totaling 4 oxygen atoms, which two O2 molecules supply exactly.
Counting 6 oxygen atoms double-counts the CO2 oxygen; the right side holds only 4.
The 4 counts hydrogen atoms in water, not oxygen atoms available from O2.

items.stem: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. Which reaction type is this?
items.rationale: An element (Zn) displaces a different element (H) from a compound, and the displaced element emerges as a free element. This is a single replacement reaction.
distractor_rationales: Synthesis would merge the reactants into a single product, but here two products form.
Decomposition needs one lone reactant breaking apart; this equation has two reactants.
Zinc, a free element, displaces hydrogen from the compound HCl, pushing hydrogen out as an element. That swap defines single replacement.
Double replacement requires two compounds trading ions; zinc is an element, not a compound.

items.stem: For the balanced equation ___ Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3, what coefficient belongs in front of Al?
items.rationale: Count atoms on the product side: 2Al2O3 contains 4 Al atoms, so 4 Al are needed on the left. The balanced equation is 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3.
distractor_rationales: One Al atom cannot supply the aluminum in two formula units of Al2O3.
This copies the subscript 2 inside Al2O3, but subscripts count atoms within a formula, not molecules needed.
This copies the coefficient 3 from O2; aluminum and oxygen coefficients balance different elements.
Two formula units of Al2O3 contain 4 Al atoms total, so 4 Al atoms must appear on the reactant side.

items.stem: C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O. Which classification fits this reaction?
items.rationale: A hydrocarbon (propane) reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water, the signature products of a combustion reaction.
distractor_rationales: Single replacement needs an element displacing another from a compound; both reactants here are small molecules, not element plus compound.
Double replacement needs two compounds exchanging ions, producing two new compounds as partners swap.
A hydrocarbon fuel reacting with oxygen to yield carbon dioxide and water is the defining pattern of a combustion reaction.
Decomposition requires a single reactant breaking into multiple products; there are two reactants here.

items.stem: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq). Which reaction type is shown?
items.rationale: Two compounds in solution trade partners: Ag+ joins Cl− to form insoluble AgCl while Na+ pairs with nitrate. Ion exchange between two compounds is double replacement.
distractor_rationales: Synthesis would yield one combined product; two distinct products form here.
No single reactant is breaking apart, so decomposition does not apply.
Single replacement requires a free element displacing another; both reactants are compounds trading ions.
The two ionic compounds exchange partners: Ag+ pairs with Cl− to precipitate AgCl while Na+ joins nitrate. That partner swap defines double replacement.

items.stem: Balance the combustion of ethane: C2H6 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. Using the smallest whole-number coefficients, what is the sum of ALL coefficients in the balanced equation?
items.rationale: First balance: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O. Sum every coefficient: 2 + 7 + 4 + 6 = 19.
distractor_rationales: This uses 6O2 after doubling 3O2 but forgetting the extra half molecule, leaving oxygen unbalanced; it sums to 18.
Balancing gives fractional coefficients first, then doubling everything: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O, and 2 + 7 + 4 + 6 = 19.
This halves the water coefficient to 3, leaving 6 hydrogen atoms on each side unbalanced; it sums to 16.
This omits the O2 coefficient from the sum: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12, but every species counts.

items.stem: Solid aluminum reacts with aqueous copper(II) sulfate: Al + CuSO4 → Al2(SO4)3 + Cu. When balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of CuSO4?
items.rationale: Treat sulfate as a unit: Al2(SO4)3 holds 3 sulfates, so 3 CuSO4 units are needed, which also releases 3 Cu. Balanced: 2Al + 3CuSO4 → Al2(SO4)3 + 3Cu.
