distractor_rationales: Three CuSO4 units supply the three sulfate groups in Al2(SO4)3, and copper balances as 3Cu, giving 2Al + 3CuSO4 → Al2(SO4)3 + 3Cu.
Treating the equation as written leaves aluminum and sulfate unbalanced, since the product needs two Al and three sulfate groups.
This copies the subscript 2 from Al2(SO4)3, but the subscript 3 outside the parentheses shows three sulfates are required.
This doubles the aluminum coefficient of 2 and wrongly copies 4 to CuSO4, oversupplying sulfate.

llm_review.issues: No substantive issues; key and rationale are correct.

exit_infection_control.title: Standard and transmission-based precautions
exit_infection_control.intro_markdown: Standard precautions apply to every client, every time: hand hygiene, gloves when touching blood or body fluids, and safe handling of sharps and soiled equipment. When a suspected or confirmed infection spreads beyond standard measures, transmission-based precautions are layered on top. Airborne precautions (TB, measles, varicella) require an N95 or higher respirator and a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room. Droplet precautions (influenza, pertussis, meningococcus) require a surgical mask within about 6 feet of the client. Contact precautions (MRSA, C. difficile, draining wounds) require gown and gloves and dedicated equipment. Correct PPE sequence when donning is gown, then mask/respirator, then eye protection, then gloves; when doffing, gloves come off first. Remember that C. difficile spores resist alcohol-based hand rubs, so soap and water is required. Worked example: a client with influenza needs droplet precautions — don a surgical mask before entering the room and perform hand hygiene on exit.
key_points: Standard precautions apply to all clients regardless of diagnosis; transmission-based precautions are added for suspected or confirmed contagious disease.

Airborne: N95 respirator plus negative-pressure room (TB, measles, varicella). Droplet: surgical mask within 6 feet (influenza, pertussis, meningococcal meningitis). Contact: gown and gloves plus dedicated equipment (MRSA, C. difficile).
Don PPE in order: gown, mask/respirator, eye protection, gloves. Remove contaminated-to-clean: gloves first, then goggles, gown, mask, and hand hygiene last.
Alcohol-based hand rub does not kill C. difficile spores; use soap and water.
After a needlestick or body-fluid exposure, wash the site first, then report and follow facility protocol.

items.stem: A client is admitted with confirmed influenza. Which personal protective equipment should the nurse don before entering the client's room?
options: Don a surgical mask before entering the room
Don an N95 respirator before entering the room
Place the client in a negative-airflow room
Wear gloves only when touching the client
items.rationale: Influenza spreads by large respiratory droplets, so droplet precautions apply. A surgical mask worn before entering the room is the required barrier.
distractor_rationales: Correct: droplet precautions require a surgical mask applied before entering the room, since influenza spreads via large droplets within about 6 feet.
An N95 is used for airborne pathogens such as TB or measles; influenza is droplet-spread, so this exceeds the requirement.
Droplet transmission does not require negative airflow; that is an airborne precaution element.
Gloves alone do not block respiratory droplets and ignore the required mask for droplet precautions.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is not PPE and is a room-placement measure, not equipment the nurse dons. N95 is not routinely required for seasonal influenza unless aerosol-generating procedures are performed.

items.stem: The nurse is about to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. In which order should personal protective equipment be applied?
items.rationale: Correct donning sequence is gown first, then mask/respirator, then eye protection, then gloves last so cuffs stay covered.
distractor_rationales: Gloves are donned last because they must cover gown cuffs and be removed first when contaminated.
Correct: gown first, then mask or respirator, then goggles or face shield, then gloves.
Eye protection is applied after the mask, not before the gown.
Removing gloves first is correct when doffing, not donning, so this reverses the sequences.

items.stem: An adult presents to the emergency department with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a new maculopapular rash that started on the face. Which room assignment is most appropriate?
options: A private room with the door closed and a surgical mask
A semi-private room with the roommate wearing a mask
A negative-airflow private room with an N95 respirator
A private room with standard precautions only
items.rationale: Suspected measles requires airborne precautions: a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room and an N95 or higher respirator for staff.
distractor_rationales: A private room with the door closed is used for droplet precautions, but measles droplet nuclei remain suspended and require negative airflow.
A semi-private room exposes the roommate to airborne spread; measles demands a private isolation room.
Correct: measles is airborne; a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room with an N95 is required.
Standard precautions alone are insufficient for any suspected communicable airborne disease.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is best; N95 is staff PPE rather than part of the room assignment, but it correctly reflects airborne precautions for suspected measles.

items.stem: A client has a positive Clostridioides difficile toxin assay and frequent watery diarrhea. Which isolation practice should the nurse implement?
options: Contact precautions with a shared bathroom and alcohol-based hand rub
Negative-pressure airborne isolation room with gown and gloves
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask and alcohol-based hand rub
Contact precautions with gown, gloves, and soap-and-water hand hygiene
items.rationale: C. difficile requires contact precautions. Hand hygiene must be with soap and water because alcohol-based rub does not inactivate spores.
distractor_rationales: The shared bathroom risks cross-contamination of other clients despite correct hand hygiene.
An unoccupied negative-pressure room wastes a scarce airborne isolation resource that C. difficile does not require.
Alcohol-based hand rub does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water is required.
Correct: contact precautions with gown, gloves, dedicated equipment, and soap-and-water hand hygiene after care.

items.stem: While recapping a used needle, a nurse sustains a deep needlestick from a client whose hepatitis B status is unknown. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Wash the puncture site thoroughly with soap and water
Obtain consent and test the source client for HIV immediately
Complete an occupational exposure report before leaving the unit
Apply a second pair of gloves over the punctured glove
items.rationale: After a needlestick, first aid comes first: wash the site with soap and water, then report the exposure and follow facility protocol for evaluation.
distractor_rationales: Correct: immediate first aid is washing the site with soap and water; report and follow-up come after.
Testing the client for HIV without consent first is inappropriate; immediate care of the nurse comes first.
Report completion is necessary but delays the essential first action of cleansing the wound.
Double-gloving is a preventive strategy, not a response after an exposure.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is implausible and weakens distractor quality; key and rationale are correct.

items.stem: A client arrives at the medical unit with night sweats, a 3-week cough, and hemoptysis; pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Obtain IV access and begin antibiotic therapy
Place a surgical mask on the client and start care
Don an N95 respirator and place the client in a negative-airflow room
Perform hand hygiene and apply sterile gloves
items.rationale: Suspected pulmonary TB is airborne: don the N95 before entering, place the client in negative-pressure isolation, then proceed with assessments and treatment.
distractor_rationales: Starting the IV antibiotic can wait until isolation is established; it delays protection of others.
A surgical mask does not filter droplet nuclei; an N95 is needed for airborne precautions.
Correct: an N95 applied before entry, then placement in negative-pressure isolation, then care activities.
Hand hygiene is essential but alone does not protect against airborne droplet nuclei.

items.stem: A client in a long-term care facility develops sudden vomiting and watery diarrhea, and norovirus is suspected. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Obtain a stool specimen for testing
Don a gown and gloves and initiate contact precautions
Don an N95 respirator before entering the room
Complete a full set of vital signs before touching the client
items.rationale: Norovirus spreads by the fecal-oral route via contaminated surfaces, so contact precautions come first; specimen collection and assessment follow once PPE is in place.
distractor_rationales: Obtaining a stool specimen is a valid task but can be done after transmission-based precautions are in place.
Correct: the first action is initiating contact precautions, including gown and gloves, before further care.
Wearing an N95 protects against airborne spread, which norovirus does not demonstrate; this misclassifies the mode of transmission.
Vital signs are part of assessment and can be obtained after precautions are initiated while wearing proper PPE.

items.stem: The nurse is assigning rooms and must determine which client requires placement in the airborne infection isolation room. Which client has that need?
options: A school-age child with influenza A
A client with a draining methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus wound
A client with a cough and a positive TB skin test and sputum smear
items.rationale: Only pulmonary tuberculosis is spread via airborne droplet nuclei requiring negative-pressure isolation and an N95; the others require droplet or contact precautions.
distractor_rationales: Influenza is spread by droplets and requires only a surgical mask, not airborne precautions.
Scabies is transmitted by close contact and requires contact precautions, not an airborne isolation room.
A draining MRSA wound requires contact precautions with gown and gloves.
Correct: pulmonary TB requires airborne precautions with negative-pressure isolation and an N95 respirator.

exit_priority_abc.title: Prioritization with airway, breathing, circulation
exit_priority_abc.intro_markdown: When several clients need help at once, the ABC rule—airway, breathing, circulation—sets the order of priority. Airway comes first because a blocked airway kills in minutes; next is effective breathing, then circulation, including bleeding and perfusion. After ABCs, use acute over chronic, new over familiar, and life-threatening over routine. Example: one client has noisy gurgling respirations while another reports incisional pain rated 8/10. Gurgling signals an obstructed airway, so that client is seen first, then pain is addressed.
key_points: Airway always comes first: gurgling, stridor, choking, or an unresponsive client outranks pain, fever, or drainage.
Breathing comes next: rising respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, low SpO2, or cyanosis takes priority over circulation and routine tasks.
Circulation follows: uncontrolled bleeding, absent pulses, or signs of shock come after airway and breathing are secured.
Apply ABCs within the first minutes of any collapse before assessing pain, medication needs, or scheduled tasks.
Within ABC, choose actual over potential: act on noisy or absent breathing before laboratory values or history findings.

items.stem: Four clients call for a nurse at the same time. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: Suction the mouth and nose with a Yankauer device.
Anticipate emergency intubation and gather equipment.
Open the airway with a jaw-thrust maneuver and position the client.
items.rationale: A responsive-to-nothing client who is not breathing needs an open airway before all else. Airway always precedes breathing and circulation.
distractor_rationales: Suctioning is appropriate for oral secretions, but an absent airway reflex requires positioning and immediate airway support first; suction alone will not protect the airway.
Anticipating intubation is a reasonable later step, but the nurse must first act to open and protect the airway with positioning; waiting for equipment delays care.
The airway is the top priority and the client is not breathing, so jaw thrust and positioning to open the airway come before any other action.
Checking the pulse assesses circulation, which is addressed only after airway and breathing are established.

items.stem: Which client should the nurse respond to first after receiving the change-of-shift report?
options: A postoperative client rating pain as 6/10 after abdominal surgery.
A client with pneumonia whose pulse oximeter reads 85% and who is using accessory muscles to breathe.
A client whose surgical dressing shows a small amount of serosanguineous drainage.
A client with a fever of 38.2°C that started yesterday.
items.rationale: An SpO2 of 85% with accessory muscle use shows breathing compromise, which is an ABC emergency outranking pain, drainage, and low-grade fever.
distractor_rationales: Rating pain is not the same as rating oxygenation; 6/10 pain can wait when another client is struggling to breathe.
Pulse oximetry of 85% with accessory muscle use indicates impaired breathing, which is second in the ABC hierarchy and outranks pain and drainage.
Drainage on a surgical dressing is expected after surgery and requires reinforcement, not urgent ABC-level attention.
A day-old fever is important but is an established problem, not a new breathing compromise.

items.stem: The nurse is assigned four stable clients but hears a new sound from one room. Which finding takes priority?
options: A client whose respirations are gurgling and noisy.
A client with new petechiae on both forearms.
A client with absent bowel sounds in all quadrants.
A client reporting unrelieved knee pain at 7/10.
items.rationale: Gurgling respirations suggest airway obstruction by secretions or the tongue; clearing the airway is the first priority in the ABC framework.
distractor_rationales: Gurgling or wet respirations signal secretions or partial obstruction in the airway, an immediate life threat that must be cleared before all else.
Petechiae are a concerning finding but reflect a circulation/skin issue that does not obstruct airflow.
Decreased bowel sounds represent a gastrointestinal assessment, lowest priority among these findings.
Unrelieved pain is real and treatable but does not threaten the airway.

items.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients. Which client should be assessed first?
options: A client whose hematocrit dropped from 36% to 30% since yesterday.
An alert client with a blood glucose of 58 mg/dL awaiting oral juice.
A client whose peripheral IV has infiltrated and stopped infusing.
A client with copious bleeding from the mouth after a tonsillectomy.
items.rationale: Active oral bleeding can obstruct and be aspirated into the airway, making it the ABC priority over anemia, mild hypoglycemia, and an IV problem.
distractor_rationales: The laboratory value is concerning for anemia and needs follow-up, but labs reflect internal status and do not stop breathing; it is third after ABC.
The blood glucose of 58 mg/dL needs treatment with juice or gel, but the client is alert; it does not outrank a compromised airway.
An infiltrated IV line can be restarted after the more urgent client with the obstructed airway is stabilized.
Copious, uncontrolled oral bleeding threatens the airway directly; blood can obstruct and can be aspirated, so this client is seen first.

items.stem: A client with a SpO2 of 88%, cyanotic lips, and labored respirations of 32/min has a strong, regular pulse. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute.
Apply oxygen and raise the head of the bed.
Document the cyanosis and oxygen saturation.
items.rationale: Cyanosis with SpO2 88% and labored breathing is a breathing emergency. The nurse applies oxygen and positions the client first, then notifies the provider.
distractor_rationales: The strong, regular pulse tells you circulation is intact; counting the respiratory rate confirms the breathing rate but does not open an airway or improve oxygenation.
An SpO2 of 88% with cyanosis and labored breathing means ineffective gas exchange; applying oxygen is the immediate ABC-based action.
Documenting can wait until urgent care is delivered; it does not treat the client.
Notifying the provider is appropriate but follows initial nursing actions that directly address breathing; calling first delays intervention.

items.stem: A client arrives at a walk-in clinic with a deep, actively bleeding forearm laceration. The client is awake and talking in full sentences with pink nail beds. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Complete a full pain assessment before touching the wound.
Establish a large-bore IV line for fluid replacement.
Apply sustained direct pressure to the bleeding site with a gloved hand.
Ask an unlicensed assistant to practice applying a tourniquet on a coworker while the nurse assesses the wound.
items.rationale: Massive external bleeding is a circulation emergency. Direct, continuous pressure is the immediate, evidence-based first action to stop the blood loss.
distractor_rationales: Assessing pain is caring but follows stabilization; circulating blood is the fluid of life and must be stopped first.
Obtaining IV access is a circulation step but comes after direct pressure; pressure controls the blood loss that threatens circulation now.
Sustained direct pressure stops external hemorrhage, which is the circulation priority before any other task.
Practicing on a coworker is irresponsible and delays care of an actual emergency.

llm_review.issues: Option 4 is unsafe and outside scope; not a credible distractor. Otherwise the keyed answer is correct.

items.stem: The nurse is assigned four clients at the start of a shift. Which client must the nurse assess first?
options: A client found unresponsive with slow, agonal respirations.
A client with an ileostomy whose output has increased to 800 mL in 4 hours.
A client with a serum potassium of 3.2 mEq/L.
A client whose temperature is 38.5°C this morning.
items.rationale: An unresponsive client with agonal respirations has both airway and breathing failing, the two highest ABC priorities, so this client must be assessed first.
distractor_rationales: Loss of consciousness with agonal respirations means the airway and breathing are already failing; this client needs immediate assessment and airway support and is the first to see.
A rising ileostomy output is a fluid and electrolyte concern; it is important but does not compromise the airway.
Serum potassium of 3.2 mEq/L requires replacement but is a laboratory abnormality addressed after unstable clients are assessed.
A fever of 38.5°C needs evaluation but is a circulation-level, non-airway concern lower in the hierarchy.

items.stem: A client receiving continuous enteral tube feedings begins to vomit. The client is now gurgling audibly and struggling to breathe. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Loosen the tape securing the feeding tube.
Check the feeding tube for placement and residual volume.
Suction the oropharynx and position the client on the side.
items.rationale: Gurgling with breathing difficulty after vomiting indicates airway threat from aspirated material; suctioning and side-lying positioning protect the airway first.
distractor_rationales: Loosening the feeding tube is premature; the change after vomiting may not represent a displaced tube until bedside verification, but the airway is being threatened now.
Stopping the feeding is appropriate to prevent further aspiration but does not clear what is already in the airway, so it comes second.
Checking residual volume addresses prevention of future aspiration but does nothing for the current obstructed airway, so it is later still.
The client has audible gurgling and difficulty breathing, meaning the airway is threatened now; suctioning is the immediate ABC-based action.

grammar_agreement.title: Subject-verb and pronoun-antecedent agreement
grammar_agreement.intro_markdown: Agreement means matching two parts of a sentence in number: a verb must agree with its true subject, and a pronoun must agree with its antecedent (the word it replaces). The trap on exams is that extra words sit between the subject and the verb. In "The list of medications is long," the subject is "list," not "medications," so the verb is singular. Ignore prepositional phrases when checking agreement. A few patterns to memorize: subjects joined by "and" usually take a plural verb; with "either/or" and "neither/nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it; indefinite pronouns such as "each," "every," and "everyone" are singular; and collective nouns like "staff" or "team" are treated as singular in formal writing. For pronouns, find the antecedent first, then match its number exactly.
key_points: Cross out prepositional phrases to find the true subject before choosing a verb.
Subjects joined by 'and' are plural; with 'either/or' and 'neither/nor,' agree with the nearer subject.
'Each,' 'every,' and 'everyone' are singular and take singular verbs and pronouns.
Collective nouns such as 'staff' and 'team' are singular in formal writing.
A pronoun must match its antecedent in number, even when other nouns intervene.

items.stem: The list of medications ______ on the chart at the bedside.
items.rationale: The subject is the singular noun 'list'; 'of medications' is a prepositional phrase and never controls the verb. Singular subject takes the singular verb 'is listed.'
distractor_rationales: This is attraction error: the verb was made plural to match 'medications' inside the prepositional phrase, not the true subject 'list.'
Correct: the true subject is the singular noun 'list,' so it takes the singular verb 'is listed.'
'Were' is plural and also past tense, but the sentence calls for the singular present tense verb.
This plural verb was pulled from 'medications' and adds an unnecessary perfect tense.

items.stem: Heart rate and respiratory rate ______ at least every four hours.
items.rationale: Two subjects joined by 'and' (heart rate and respiratory rate) form a plural compound subject, which requires the plural verb 'are recorded.'
distractor_rationales: 'Is' is singular, but a compound subject joined by 'and' is plural.
'Was' is both singular and past tense; neither fits a compound present-tense subject.
Correct: 'Heart rate and respiratory rate' is a compound subject joined by 'and,' so it takes the plural verb 'are recorded.'
'Has been recorded' is singular and perfect tense; the plural compound subject needs a plural present-tense verb.

items.stem: Either the residents or their families ______ to the care conference.
items.rationale: In 'either/or' and 'neither/nor' constructions, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. 'Families' is plural, so the plural verb 'are invited' is correct.
distractor_rationales: Correct: with 'either/or,' the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it; 'families' is plural, so 'are invited' is correct.
'Is' would agree only with the singular 'residents,' which is the farther subject and does not control the verb.
'Was' is both singular and past tense, so it fails on number and tense.
'Will be inviting' changes the meaning; the families receive the invitation rather than give it.

items.stem: Each of the patients ______ an identification bracelet before transfer.
items.rationale: The subject is the indefinite pronoun 'each,' which is always singular even though 'patients' is plural. The object of a prepositional phrase never controls the verb, so the singular 'wears' is correct.
distractor_rationales: 'Wear' is plural; the true subject 'each' is singular, so the verb must be singular.
'Are wearing' matches 'patients' inside the phrase, but the object of 'of' never controls the verb.
'Have worn' is plural and perfect tense; neither matches the singular subject 'each.'
Correct: 'Each' is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes the singular verb 'wears.'

items.stem: Every patient must update ______ contact information before the appointment.
items.rationale: The antecedent 'every patient' is singular; 'every' always creates a singular reference. Formal written English requires the singular pronoun 'his or her' to match.
distractor_rationales: 'Their' is plural, but 'every patient' is a singular antecedent in formal written English.
Correct: the singular antecedent 'every patient' takes the singular pronoun 'his or her' in formal grammar.
'Them' is plural and also an object pronoun, so it fails to agree and is the wrong case.
'Its' is singular but refers to nonhuman antecedents; a patient is a person, not a thing.

items.stem: The nursing staff ______ required to attend the in-service on Friday.
items.rationale: 'Staff' is a collective noun treated as singular in formal writing because the group acts as one unit here, so it takes the singular verb 'is required.'
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'staff' is a collective noun acting as one unit, so it takes the singular verb 'is required.'
'Are' treats the staff as separate individuals; formal writing keeps the collective noun singular.
'Were being' is plural and awkwardly passive; the singular present-tense verb is needed.
'Have been' is plural, matching the writers' sense of many employees rather than one unit.

items.stem: The results of the urinalysis ______ within normal limits.
items.rationale: The true subject is the plural noun 'results'; 'of the urinalysis' is only a prepositional phrase. A plural subject takes the plural verb 'were.'
distractor_rationales: 'Was' is singular; it was likely pulled from the idea of one test rather than the plural subject 'results.'
'Is' is singular and present tense; the subject is plural and the context is past.
Correct: the subject 'results' is plural, so it takes the plural past-tense verb 'were.'
'Has been' is singular; it also mismatches the plural 'results.'

items.stem: Neither the surgeon nor the technicians have finished ______ reports.
items.rationale: In a 'neither/nor' construction, both the verb and pronoun agree with the nearer antecedent. 'Technicians' is plural, matching the plural verb 'have' and the pronoun 'their.'
distractor_rationales: 'His or her' is singular, but the nearer antecedent 'technicians' is plural and controls the pronoun.
'His' is singular and assumes all technicians are male; it fails to agree with the plural antecedent.
'Its' refers to nonhuman antecedents and is singular; people cannot be called 'its.'
Correct: with 'neither/nor,' the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, the plural 'technicians,' so 'their' is correct.

grammar_confused_words.title: Commonly confused words (affect/effect, their/there, lie/lay)
grammar_confused_words.intro_markdown: Many spelling mix-ups involve short words that sound alike. "Affect" is usually a verb meaning to influence: "Stress can affect blood pressure." "Effect" is usually a noun meaning a result: "The medication had a soothing effect." "Their" shows possession, "there" points to a place, and "they're" is short for "they are." "Lie" means to recline and takes no object ("I lie down"), while "lay" means to put something down and takes an object ("I lay the chart on the desk"). A quick check: if you can substitute a form of "to place" and the sentence still works, use "lay." If you can substitute "to recline," use "lie."
key_points: Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence; effect is usually a noun meaning a result.
Their shows possession, there indicates a place, and they're is the contraction of they are.
Lie means to recline and takes no object; lay means to put something down and takes an object.
The past tense of lie is lay; the past tense of lay is laid.
Affect can be a noun in psychology (observable mood), and effect can be a verb meaning to bring about, but these uses are less common.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: The nurse explained that low potassium levels can ______ a patient's heart rhythm.
options: Lack of sleep can effect a patient's ability to heal.
Lack of sleep can affect a patient's ability to heal.
Lack of sleep can affectation a patient's ability to heal.
Lack of sleep can effects a patient's ability to heal.
items.rationale: After the modal verb 'can,' a main verb is needed. 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'to influence,' so it correctly completes the sentence.
distractor_rationales: Uses the noun form where the sentence needs the verb meaning 'to influence.'
Correct: 'affect' is the verb meaning 'to influence,' which fits after the modal 'can.'
Uses the noun form where the verb is required.
Not a standard word in this context; it is a misspelling of the verb form.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: The new nursing students left the orientation packets over ______.
options: The new students were assigned rooms over they're.
The new students were assigned rooms over their.
The new students were assigned rooms over there.
The new students were assigned rooms over theirs.
items.rationale: The sentence needs a word pointing to a location. 'There' is the adverb of place; 'their' is possessive and 'they're' means 'they are.'
distractor_rationales: 'They're' means 'they are,' which does not fit before 'assigned rooms.'
'Their' is possessive and would wrongly make 'rooms' belong to the students.
Correct: 'there' is the adverb pointing to a location.
'Theirs' is a standalone pronoun and cannot modify a noun.

llm_review.issues: Stem and options mismatch: the stem asks to complete 'left the orientation packets over ____,' but the options complete a different sentence about assigned rooms. Option 3 remains the only grammatically correct homophone choice.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: Every staff member should label ______ supplies before the shift begins.
options: Every staff member should label their supplies before the shift begins.
Every staff member should label there supplies before the shift begins.
Every staff member should label they're supplies before the shift begins.
Every staff member should label theirs supplies before the shift begins.
items.rationale: The blank requires a possessive adjective modifying 'supplies.' 'Their' shows ownership; 'there' is a place word and 'they're' means 'they are.'
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'their' is the possessive form showing the supplies belong to the staff members.
'There' indicates place, not possession, and does not fit before a noun.
'They're' means 'they are,' which creates a nonsensical sentence.
'Theirs' stands alone and cannot modify the noun 'supplies.'

items.stem: Choose the correct verb form: The aide ______ the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
options: The aide lie the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
The aide lays the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
The aide lain the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
The aide laid the safety bars up before transferring the patient.
items.rationale: 'Lay' means to put something down and takes an object ('safety bars'). Its past tense is 'laid,' which fits this past-tense sentence.
distractor_rationales: 'Lie' takes no object; 'safety bars' would be left without a verb acting on it.
'Lays' is present tense, but the sentence needs the past-tense verb that takes an object.
'Lain' is the past participle of 'lie' and cannot take the object 'safety bars.'
Correct: 'laid' is the past tense of 'lay,' the verb meaning 'to put something down,' and takes the object 'safety bars.'

items.stem: Choose the correct word: The physician reviewed the possible side ______ of the new antibiotic before obtaining the patient's consent.
options: The charge nurse documented the patient's affect after administering the new medication.
The charge nurse documented the effects of the new medication on the patient.
The charge nurse documented the patient's affects after the new medication.
The charge nurse documented the patient's effecting after the new medication.
items.rationale: The sentence needs the plural noun meaning 'results,' which is 'effects.' 'Affect' as a noun refers to observable mood or emotional expression, not outcomes.
distractor_rationales: Uses the verb form where the noun 'result' is required.
'Effects' as a verb means 'brings about,' which would need a direct object like 'change,' not an adjective phrase.
Correct: 'effects' is the plural noun meaning 'results' or 'outcomes.'
Combines the noun form with a verb ending, creating a grammatically impossible form.

items.stem: Choose the correct verb form: After the procedure, the patient ______ in the recovery room for an hour.
options: After the procedure, the patient lain in the recovery room for an hour.
After the procedure, the patient lay in the recovery room for an hour.
After the procedure, the patient laid in the recovery room for an hour.
After the procedure, the patient laying in the recovery room for an hour.
items.rationale: 'Lie' (to recline) has the past tense 'lay.' The patient reclines, and no object follows, so 'lay' is correct here even though it looks like the present of another verb.
distractor_rationales: Reverses the tenses: 'lain' is for 'lie' and 'lay' is present tense for 'lay.'
Correct: 'lay' is the past tense of 'lie' (to recline), which needs no object.
Uses the past tense of 'lay,' which requires an object.
Adds an '-ing' ending, which does not fit with 'for an hour.'

items.stem: Choose the correct sentence with both words used properly.
options: The assessment noted that the patient's affect was flat and that the medication's effects appeared within thirty minutes.
The assessment noted that the patient's effect was flat and that the medication's affects appeared within thirty minutes.
The assessment noted that the patient's affects were flat and that the medication's effecting appeared within thirty minutes.
The assessment noted that the patient's affect was flat and that the medication's affecting appeared within thirty minutes.
items.rationale: 'Affect' as a noun means observable emotional expression ('flat affect'). 'Effects' as a plural noun means results, which fits the medication's outcomes.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'affect' (noun) means observable emotional expression, and 'effects' (noun) means results.
Uses 'effect,' which does not describe observable emotional expression.
'Affects' is a verb, not the noun needed after 'flat.'
'Affect' cannot describe emotional expression, and 'affecting' is a verb form.

items.stem: Choose the sentence in which all three commonly confused words are used correctly.
options: The patient was lying quietly when the nurse placed their call light over there.
The patient was laying quietly when the nurse placed they're call light over there.
The patient was lying quietly when the nurse placed there call light over their.
The patient was lying quietly when the nurse placed their call light over there.
items.rationale: 'Lying' correctly describes reclining without an object; 'their' shows the call light belongs to the patient; 'there' points to the location where it was placed.
distractor_rationales: 'Lying' fits the patient but 'there' is a place word and cannot modify 'call light.'
'Laying' would wrongly take the patient as an object, and 'they're' means 'they are.'
'Lying' fits, but 'their' would mean the call light belongs to the nurses rather than identifying it.
Correct: 'lying' (reclining, no object), 'their' (possessive, belonging to the patient), and 'there' (place) all fit.

grammar_parts_of_speech.title: Parts of speech
grammar_parts_of_speech.intro_markdown: Every word in an English sentence belongs to a part of speech, a category describing its job rather than its meaning. The eight main categories are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection. Nouns name people, places, things, or ideas; pronouns replace nouns; verbs show action or link subject to description; adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs; prepositions begin phrases showing relationships such as location or time; conjunctions join words or clauses; interjections express emotion. To classify a word, test its function in the sentence. Consider this worked example: in "The tired aide quickly entered the quiet ward," "aide" and "ward" are nouns, "tired" and "quiet" are adjectives, "entered" is a verb, and "quickly" is an adverb telling how the entering happened. One word can shift categories, so always analyze the role it plays in the specific sentence. Identifying parts of speech builds the foundation for spotting agreement, case, and modification errors on the exam.
key_points: Classify words by function in the sentence, not by meaning alone.
Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs.
Subject pronouns (I, he) act in subjects; object pronouns (me, him) receive action.
A gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun; the same form used to modify is a participle.
Prepositions begin phrases of relationship (location, time, direction); conjunctions join words or clauses.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is a noun? The nurse recorded the patient's temperature carefully.
items.rationale: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. "Temperature" names a thing and serves as the object of the verb "recorded."
distractor_rationales: The is an article, a special type of adjective, not a noun.
Recorded is the action verb of the sentence, showing what the nurse did.
Carefully is an adverb modifying the verb recorded, describing how the action was done.
Temperature names a thing and serves as the direct object of the verb recorded.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is a verb? The pharmacist reviewed the chart before the shift ended.
items.rationale: A verb expresses action or state of being. "Reviewed" is the action the pharmacist performed, so it is the verb of the sentence.
distractor_rationales: Reviewed expresses the action performed by the subject, making it the verb.
Pharmacist is a noun naming the person who performs the action.
Before is a preposition here, beginning the phrase before the shift.
Chart is a noun naming the object being reviewed.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is an adverb? The aide quietly opened the heavy door.
items.rationale: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. "Quietly" modifies the verb "opened," telling how the opening was done.
distractor_rationales: Quiet is an adjective describing the aide, but the sentence uses quietly to describe the action, not the noun.
Heavy is an adjective describing the noun door.
Door is a noun naming the object being opened.
Quietly modifies the verb opened, telling how the action was performed, which is the role of an adverb.

llm_review.issues: Option 1, 'quiet,' is not actually present in the sentence, making it an invalid distractor for a question asking which word in the sentence is an adverb.

items.stem: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? The director thanked the volunteer and ____ for organizing the supply closet.
items.rationale: The pronoun is part of the compound object of "thanked." Object position requires an object pronoun, so "her" is correct.
distractor_rationales: She is a subject pronoun and cannot serve as the object of the verb thanked.
Her is the object form, correctly receiving the action of the verb thanked, even when paired with a named person.
Herself is a reflexive pronoun used only when the subject acts upon itself, which does not fit here.
Hers is a possessive pronoun showing ownership, not an object receiving the action.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence functions as a preposition? The supply cart was parked beside the elevator.
items.rationale: A preposition begins a phrase showing a relationship such as location or time. "Beside" begins the phrase "beside the elevator" and tells where the cart was parked.
distractor_rationales: Parked is the verb of the sentence, expressing the action performed on the cart.
The is an article functioning as an adjective, not a preposition.
Beside begins the prepositional phrase beside the elevator, showing the relationship of location between the cart and the elevator.
Elevator is the object of the preposition, a noun, not the preposition itself.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence is a linking verb? The patient's skin remained warm throughout the evening.
items.rationale: A linking verb connects the subject to a word that describes it. "Remained" links the subject "skin" to the predicate adjective "warm" rather than showing action.
distractor_rationales: Remained is a linking verb connecting the subject skin to the predicate adjective warm.
Warm is a predicate adjective describing the subject after the linking verb.
Skin is the subject noun being described.
Evening is a noun telling when, part of the adverbial prepositional phrase.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence functions as a noun? Charting accurately takes practice.
items.rationale: A gerund is an -ing form used as a noun. "Charting" acts as the subject of the sentence, so it functions as a noun despite its verb form.
distractor_rationales: Takes is the main verb of the sentence, showing what charting does.
Accurately is an adverb modifying the gerund charting.
Practice is a noun serving as the direct object of the gerund phrase, not the gerund itself.
Charting is a gerund, an -ing verb form functioning as a noun, because it serves as the subject of the verb takes.

items.stem: Which word in the following sentence functions as a relative pronoun? The student who completed the practicum received a certificate.
items.rationale: A relative pronoun introduces a dependent clause and refers to a noun. "Who" begins the clause "who completed the practicum" and stands for "student."
distractor_rationales: The is an article functioning as an adjective modifying student.
Who is a relative pronoun introducing the clause who completed the practicum and referring back to student.
Completed is the verb of the relative clause describing the student.
Received is the main verb of the sentence, showing what the student did.

llm_review.issues: Distractors are different parts of speech and do not compete with the relative pronoun, making the item very easy.

grammar_punctuation.title: Punctuation and sentence structure
grammar_punctuation.intro_markdown: Punctuation marks do the traffic control work of English sentences. A period ends a complete sentence; a comma joins clauses only when paired with a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). A semicolon joins two complete sentences without a conjunction. Apostrophes show possession or contraction, never simple plurals. Watch for fragments (incomplete thoughts), run-ons (fused sentences), and comma splices (two sentences joined by only a comma). Example: "The nurse charted the vitals; they were stable." The semicolon correctly joins two complete thoughts.
key_points: Commas join independent clauses only with a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor).
Semicolons join two independent clauses without a conjunction.
A comma alone between two complete sentences is a comma splice—an error.
Apostrophes show possession or contractions, never simple plurals.
Introductory dependent clauses are followed by a comma; nonessential clauses take paired commas.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The aide asked. Did the patient eat breakfast?
The aide asked, did the patient eat breakfast?
The aide asked; did the patient eat breakfast?
The aide asked, did the patient eat breakfast!
items.rationale: A direct question introduced by a comma inside a sentence ends with a question mark. Only the comma before it is needed to set it off.
distractor_rationales: A period cannot replace the question mark; a direct question needs a question mark regardless of sentence position.
Correct: a direct question embedded in a sentence is set off by a comma and ends with a question mark.
A semicolon separates complete sentences; it cannot introduce a direct question.
An exclamation point signals strong emotion, which the sentence does not express.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly?
options: The shift ended, the nurse finished her notes.
The shift ended. And reviewed the chart one last time.
The shift ended, but the nurse reviewed the chart one last time.
The shift ended but, the nurse reviewed the chart one last time.
items.rationale: A comma before a coordinating conjunction (but) correctly joins two independent clauses. The comma must come before the conjunction, not after it.
distractor_rationales: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is incorrect.
A period creates a fragment because 'and reviewed the chart' has no subject and cannot stand alone.
Correct: the comma before the conjunction 'but' properly joins two complete sentences.
No punctuation before the coordinating conjunction creates a run-on (fused) sentence.

items.stem: Which sentence punctuates the introductory clause correctly?
options: After the patient stabilized, the nurse left the room.
After the patient, stabilized the nurse left the room.
After the patient stabilized; the nurse left the room.
After the patient stabilized the nurse left the room.
items.rationale: An introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma. 'After the patient stabilized' cannot stand alone, so it must be separated from the main clause.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 'after the patient stabilized' is an introductory dependent clause and needs a comma after it.
The comma incorrectly separates the clause from its verb; introductory phrases take a comma after, not before.
Semicolons cannot attach a dependent clause to the main clause.
Dependent introductory clauses require a comma; omitting it is an error.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 is an implausible distractor; item is otherwise straightforward.

items.stem: Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?
options: The unit filed three report's for the incident.
The unit filed three report for the incident.
The unit filed three report's' for the incident.
The unit filed three reports for the incident.
items.rationale: Simple plurals take no apostrophe—just add s. Apostrophes mark possession or contractions, never plurals.
distractor_rationales: No apostrophe is used in simple plurals; 'reports' merely names several documents.
The apostrophe placement here creates either a possessive or nonsense; the plural of report is reports.
Adding 's' after the apostrophe makes a singular possessive, wrong for a simple plural.
Correct: the plural of report is reports with no apostrophe.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 tests plural formation rather than apostrophe use, and option 3 is implausible, reducing distractor quality.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly joins two complete thoughts without a coordinating conjunction?
options: The medication arrived late, the pharmacy had short staffing.
The medication arrived late; the pharmacy had short staffing.
The medication arrived late: the pharmacy had short staffing.
The medication arrived late — the pharmacy had short staffing.
items.rationale: A semicolon can join two independent clauses that are closely related, with no coordinating conjunction present. The other choices create splices.
distractor_rationales: A comma splice: two independent clauses cannot be joined by only a comma.
Correct: a semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.
A colon introduces lists, quotations, or explanations, not a second independent clause of equal weight in this construction.
A dash does not correctly fuse two sentences here and creates an informal, incorrect splice.

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly around the nonessential clause?
options: The patient who was surrounded by family, rested calmly.
The patient, who was surrounded by family rested calmly.
The patient, who was surrounded by family, rested calmly.
The patient; who was surrounded by family, rested calmly.
items.rationale: A nonessential (nonrestrictive) clause must be enclosed by paired commas. It adds extra information and could be removed without changing the core meaning.
distractor_rationales: Removing both commas wrongly treats the nonessential clause as restrictive; family information is extra, not identifying.
The second comma is misplaced; nonessential clauses take commas on both sides.
Correct: the nonessential clause is enclosed with paired commas.
A semicolon cannot set off a clause inside a sentence.

llm_review.issues: Grammar-focused item rather than nursing/clinical content; keyed answer and rationale are correct.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The surgeon reviewed the scans, therefore the procedure was postponed.
The surgeon reviewed the scans. Therefore the procedure was postponed, and rescheduled.
The surgeon reviewed the scans, therefore; the procedure was postponed.
The surgeon reviewed the scans; therefore, the procedure was postponed.
items.rationale: When joining independent clauses with a conjunctive adverb like 'therefore,' use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.
distractor_rationales: A comma cannot join two independent clauses even with a conjunctive adverb; a semicolon is required before 'therefore'.
A period would leave 'therefore' starting a fragment with no complete clause after it.
A comma splice; conjunctive adverbs like 'therefore' need a semicolon before them and a comma after.
Correct: semicolon before the conjunctive adverb, comma after it.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the possessive correctly?
options: The charge nurse combined the nurses' notes into one record.
The charge nurse combined the nurses'' notes into one record.
The charge nurse combined the nurse's notes into one record.
The charge nurse combined the nurses are notes into one record.
items.rationale: For a plural noun ending in s, the possessive adds only an apostrophe after the s: nurses' notes means notes belonging to several nurses.
distractor_rationales: Correct: the possessive 'nurses' belongs with the singular noun 'note,' producing the possessive of a plural noun.
The double apostrophe creates a nonsense form; only one possessive is needed.
'Nurse's is singular possessive, but the sentence describes notes from multiple nurses.
This creates a contraction ('nurses are') where a possessive is required by the following noun 'note.'

math_algebra.title: One-variable equations and order of operations
math_algebra.intro_markdown:
Solving one-variable equations and evaluating expressions both rest on two skills: following the order of operations, and undoing operations in reverse to isolate a variable.

Order of operations (PEMDAS): Parentheses first, then Exponents, then Multiplication and Division left to right, then Addition and Subtraction left to right.

For equations, undo operations in reverse order — addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division — doing the same thing to both sides.

Worked example: a vial had x mL of saline; after 7.5 mL is removed, 12.2 mL remain. Write x − 7.5 = 12.2. Undo the subtraction by adding 7.5 to both sides: x = 12.2 + 7.5 = 19.7 mL.

For a two-step equation like 4x + 8 = 1308, subtract 8 from both sides (4x = 1300), then divide by 4 (x = 325). Always simplify each side completely using order of operations before moving terms across the equals sign.
key_points: PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right).
Undo operations in reverse order when solving: clear addition/subtraction, then multiplication/division.
Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other.
Simplify each side fully before moving variable or constant terms across the equals sign.
Check your solution by substituting it back into the original equation.

items.stem: Evaluate the expression: 8 + 4 × 3 − 6 ÷ 2
items.rationale: Multiply and divide before adding and subtracting: 4 × 3 = 12 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so 8 + 12 − 3 = 17.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 4 × 3 = 12 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 before adding and subtracting.
Incorrect: computed strictly left to right: 8 + 4 = 12, 12 × 3 = 36, 36 − 6 = 30, 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
Incorrect: added 8 + 4 before multiplying: (8 + 4) × 3 − 6 ÷ 2 = 36 − 3 = 33.
Incorrect: divided the entire expression by 2 at the end: (8 + 12 − 6) ÷ 2 = 14 ÷ 2 = 7.

items.stem: A vial containing x mL of sterile water had 7.5 mL added to it, bringing the total to 12.2 mL. Which equation solves for the original amount?
items.rationale: Subtracting 7.5 mL is undone by adding 7.5 to both sides... rather, the equation x + 7.5 = 12.2 gives x = 12.2 − 7.5 = 4.7 mL.
distractor_rationales: Incorrect: added 7.5 to 12.2 instead of subtracting; that reverses the operation described.
Correct: subtract 7.5 from both sides: x = 12.2 − 7.5 = 4.7 mL.
Incorrect: mis-borrowed during the subtraction 12.2 − 7.5, getting 4.8 instead of 4.7.
Incorrect: multiplied 7.5 × 12.2, which does not undo subtraction.

items.stem: Evaluate the expression: 2³ + 3 × (5 − 2)²
items.rationale: Parentheses first: 5 − 2 = 3. Exponents next: 3² = 9 and 2³ = 8. Then multiply: 3 × 9 = 27. Finally add: 8 + 27 = 35.
distractor_rationales: Incorrect: skipped the exponent on (5 − 2), computing 8 + 3 × 3 = 17.
Incorrect: grouped 2³ + 3 first: (8 + 3) × 9 = 99.
Incorrect: put the subtraction inside the square: 3 × 5 − 2 = 13, then 8 + 13² = 177.

llm_review.issues: Option 3 is implausible as a distractor.

items.stem: A patient's daily calcium intake from 4 equal servings of yogurt plus an 8 mg supplement totals 1,308 mg. If each serving provides x mg, what is the value of x?
items.rationale: Undo addition first: 4x + 8 = 1308, so 4x = 1300. Then divide by 4: x = 325 mg of calcium per serving.
distractor_rationales: Incorrect: divided 1308 by 4 without first subtracting the 8 mg from the supplement.
Incorrect: added 8 to 1308 before dividing; subtraction is undone by subtraction, not addition.
Incorrect: divided by 2 instead of by the coefficient 4.

items.stem: Two IV bags hold equal volumes. One bag holds 3x + 5 mL and the other holds 2x + 14 mL. What is the value of x?
items.rationale: Subtract 2x from both sides: x + 5 = 14. Then subtract 5 from both sides: x = 9 mL in each bag.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 3x − 2x = x, so x + 5 = 14 and x = 9 mL.
Incorrect: added the constants 5 + 14 and dropped the variable terms entirely.
Incorrect: combined like terms wrongly as 5x = 19, adding coefficients and constants together.
Incorrect: subtracted every number in the equation from 14 (14 − 5 − 3 − 2 = 4), mixing terms that are not alike.

items.stem: Evaluate the expression: 24 × 0.25 + 1.5 ÷ 0.5
items.rationale: Multiply and divide before adding: 24 × 0.25 = 6 and 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3, so 6 + 3 = 9.
distractor_rationales: Incorrect: worked strictly left to right: (6 + 1.5) ÷ 0.5 = 7.5 ÷ 0.5 = 15.
Incorrect: added inside the multiplication: 24 × (0.25 + 1.5) ÷ 0.5 = 42 ÷ 0.5 = 84.
Incorrect: stopped after 6 + 1.5 = 7.5 and never performed the division.
Correct: multiplication and division come before addition: 6 + 3 = 9.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 (84) is not readily explained by a common calculation error; options 1 and 3 reflect plausible order-of-operations mistakes.

items.stem: A medication order states that 5 times the quantity (x + 2) mg equals 3x + 26 mg. Solve for x.
items.rationale: Distribute first: 5x + 10 = 3x + 26. Subtract 3x: 2x + 10 = 26. Subtract 10: 2x = 16, so x = 8 mg.
distractor_rationales: Incorrect: moved the 10 with the wrong sign, getting 2x = 36 and x = 18.
Correct: 5x + 10 = 3x + 26, so 2x = 16 and x = 8 mg.
Incorrect: forgot to subtract 10 from 26, solving 2x = 26 for x = 13.
Incorrect: added 2 to 26 before dividing, solving 2x = 28 for x = 14.

llm_review.issues: Distractors correspond to common algebra errors, but the medication-order framing is unnecessary and adds no clinical context.

items.stem: A nurse records a patient's 24-hour intake using the expression 3 × (120 + 45) − 240 ÷ 8. Evaluate to find the intake in mL.
items.rationale: Parentheses first: 120 + 45 = 165. Then 3 × 165 = 495 and 240 ÷ 8 = 30. Subtract last: 495 − 30 = 465 mL.
distractor_rationales: Incorrect: worked strictly left to right: 495 − 240 = 255, then 255 ÷ 8 ≈ 31.9.
Incorrect: moved the division inside the parentheses: 3 × (165 − 30) = 3 × 135 = 405.
Correct: parentheses first, then 3 × 165 = 495 and 240 ÷ 8 = 30, so 495 − 30 = 465.
Incorrect: added the 30 instead of subtracting it from 495.

math_conversions.title: Metric and household measurement conversions used in health care
math_conversions.intro_markdown: Health-care math runs on a small set of fixed conversion facts, and most errors come from memorizing them loosely rather than exactly. The metric relationships are powers of 1,000: 1 g = 1,000 mg and 1 L = 1,000 mL. The household-to-metric facts you must hold precisely are 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 tbsp = 15 mL (so 3 tsp = 1 tbsp), 1 fluid ounce = 30 mL, 1 cup = 240 mL, and 1 lb = 16 oz. Weight bridges metric and household: 1 kg = 2.2 lb. To go from pounds to kilograms, divide by 2.2; to go the other way, multiply by 2.2. Height uses 1 in = 2.54 cm, and feet must first become inches (1 ft = 12 in). A worked example: an infant weighs 13.2 lb. Divide 13.2 by 2.2 to get 6 kg. If the ordered dose is 15 mg per kg, multiply 6 kg by 15 mg to get 90 mg. Write each step down so the units cancel and the arithmetic stays checkable.
key_points: 1 kg = 2.2 lb; divide pounds by 2.2 to get kilograms, multiply to go back
Household equivalents: 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 tbsp = 15 mL, 1 fl oz = 30 mL, 1 cup = 240 mL
Metric prefixes shift by 1,000: 1 g = 1,000 mg and 1 L = 1,000 mL
1 ft = 12 in and 1 in = 2.54 cm; convert feet to inches before converting to centimeters
Track units through every step so a wrong conversion direction is visible immediately

items.stem: A nurse prepares a dose of 2 g of a medication. How many milligrams is this?
items.rationale: Each gram contains 1,000 mg, so 2 g × 1,000 mg/g = 2,000 mg.
distractor_rationales: Divides by 1,000, reversing the prefix relationship for grams to milligrams.
Treats the step as a factor of 10 instead of 1,000.
Multiplies 2 by 1,000 because each gram contains 1,000 milligrams.
Adds three zeros without changing the unit label, leaving a magnitude error.

items.stem: A liquid medication is measured as 30 mL. Using the household equivalent 1 tbsp = 15 mL, how many tablespoons is this?
items.rationale: One tablespoon holds 15 mL, so 30 mL ÷ 15 mL/tbsp = 2 tbsp.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 30 mL ÷ 15 mL per tablespoon equals 2 tablespoons.
Divides by 5 instead of 15, confusing the teaspoon equivalent.
Multiplies 30 by 15, inverting the conversion factor.
Divides by 30, using the ounce equivalent instead of the tablespoon equivalent.

items.stem: An IV bag contains 0.5 L of fluid. How many milliliters is that?
items.rationale: One liter equals 1,000 mL, so 0.5 L × 1,000 = 500 mL.
distractor_rationales: Drops two zeros, treating the prefix step as a factor of 10.
Reverses the direction by dividing instead of multiplying.
Treats a liter as 10 mL rather than 1,000 mL.
Multiplies by 1,000 because one liter contains 1,000 milliliters.

llm_review.issues: Distractors are implausibly small for an IV bag and are not tightly targeted to a consistent conversion mistake.

items.stem: An infant admitted to the pediatric unit weighs 13.2 lb. What is the weight in kilograms, rounded to the nearest whole number?
items.rationale: Pounds become kilograms by dividing by 2.2: 13.2 ÷ 2.2 = 6 kg.
distractor_rationales: Converts the other direction, multiplying pounds by 2.2 instead of dividing.
Correct: 13.2 lb ÷ 2.2 lb per kilogram equals 6 kg.
Uses 2.5 as the conversion factor instead of 2.2.
Subtracts 2.2 from the pound weight rather than dividing by it.

llm_review.issues: Option 2 is correct: 13.2 lb ÷ 2.2 ≈ 6 kg. Option 1 reflects multiplying instead of dividing; option 3 is not rounded to the nearest whole number and uses an incorrect conversion factor.

items.stem: A client on a fluid-intake record drinks 2 cups of water at lunch. Using 1 cup = 240 mL, how many milliliters did the client drink?
items.rationale: Two cups at 240 mL each give 2 × 240 = 480 mL.
distractor_rationales: Treats a cup as 120 mL, half the standard household equivalent.
Uses 300 mL per cup, an overstated equivalent.
Correct: 240 mL per cup times 2 cups equals 480 mL.
Uses 500 mL per cup, rounding the equivalence far too high.

items.stem: A child who weighs 33 lb is prescribed an antibiotic at 15 mg per kg of body weight. What total dose, in mg, should the nurse calculate?
items.rationale: 33 lb ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg; then 15 mg/kg × 15 kg = 225 mg.
distractor_rationales: Correct: 33 ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg, then 15 × 15 = 225 mg.
Stops after the weight conversion and reports kilograms as the dose.
Converts pounds by multiplying by 2.2, then computes the per-kilogram dose on 72.6 kg.
Divides 33 by 2.5 instead of 2.2, giving 13.2 kg before applying the dose factor.

llm_review.issues: Options 3 and 4 are not clearly based on common conversion or dosage errors; option 2 is a plausible distractor for omitting weight.

items.stem: During a 12-hour shift, a client drinks 1 cup of broth, 6 oz of juice, and receives 500 mL of IV fluid. Using 1 oz = 30 mL, what is the total intake in milliliters?
items.rationale: Broth 1 cup = 240 mL; juice 6 oz × 30 = 180 mL; IV 500 mL; total 240 + 180 + 500 = 920 mL.
distractor_rationales: Omits the juice entirely, counting only the broth and IV fluid.
Uses 15 mL per ounce (the tablespoon equivalent) for the juice, and also drops the broth: 6 × 15 + 500 = 590 mL.
Uses 200 mL per cup for the broth, understating that term: 200 + 180 + 500 = 880 mL.
Correct: 240 + 180 + 500 = 920 mL for the shift.

llm_review.issues: The 1 cup = 8 oz conversion is not explicitly stated, though it is standard in nursing intake calculations.

items.stem: A client's height is documented as 5 ft 8 in. What is this height in centimeters, rounded to one decimal place?
distractor_rationales: Converts only the 8 inches to centimeters and ignores the feet portion.
Correct: 68 inches times 2.54 centimeters per inch gives 172.72, which rounds to 172.7 cm.
Forgets to convert feet to inches first and multiplies 5 by 2.54 before adding 8 cm.
Rounds to 173 and then adds an extra unit, pushing the value above the true height.

llm_review.issues: Options 1 and 3 are implausibly small for adult height; option 4 is an approximation and is not rounded to one decimal place.

math_decimals_percents.title: Decimals and percents, converting between forms
math_decimals_percents.intro_markdown: Decimals and percents are two ways of writing the same kind of number, so nursing math depends on moving between them smoothly. To turn a decimal into a percent, multiply by 100 and attach the percent sign; 0.45 becomes 45%. To turn a percent into a decimal, drop the percent sign and divide by 100; 7% becomes 0.07. Watch the decimal point: each move across one place changes the value tenfold, so 0.07 and 0.7 are very different drug strengths. A percent is also "out of 100," which makes finding a percent of a quantity a multiplication problem. For example, if a patient drank 0.6 of a 250 mL cup of water, multiply 0.6 × 250 to get 150 mL. Percent change and finding an original amount add one more layer: identify the correct base number before you calculate, because using the wrong base is the most common error.
key_points: Decimal to percent: multiply by 100 (shift the decimal point two places right).
Percent to decimal: divide by 100 (shift the decimal point two places left).
Percent of a quantity: convert the percent to a decimal, then multiply.
Part ÷ whole × 100 gives the percent one number is of another.
In percent change and find-the-whole problems, always identify the correct base before calculating.

items.stem: Write 0.45 as a percent.
items.rationale: Multiply the decimal by 100 (move the point two places right): 0.45 × 100 = 45, so 0.45 = 45%.
distractor_rationales: 4.5% comes from moving the decimal only one place, which divides by 10 instead of 100 in reverse.
0.45 × 100 = 45, so moving the decimal two places right gives the percent.
0.45% treats the decimal as if it were already a percent; the value stays essentially unchanged.
450% comes from moving the decimal two places right and then multiplying by 10 again.

items.stem: A topical ointment is labeled 7% active ingredient. Written as a decimal, 7% equals which value?
items.rationale: Drop the percent sign and divide by 100: 7 ÷ 100 = 0.07, so 7% = 0.07 as a decimal.
distractor_rationales: 7% means 7 per 100, so divide by 100: 7 ÷ 100 = 0.07.
0.7 equals 70%, a tenfold overdose of the decimal shift.
7.0 is just the whole number 7 written as a decimal, which equals 700%.
0.007 equals 0.7%, from shifting the point three places instead of two.

items.stem: A patient drank 0.6 of a 250 mL cup of water during a shift. How many milliliters did the patient drink?
items.rationale: Taking 0.6 of a quantity means multiplying: 0.6 × 250 mL = 150 mL consumed.
distractor_rationales: 60 mL comes from subtracting 0.6 from 250 instead of multiplying by 0.6.
15 mL comes from treating 0.6 as 0.06 when multiplying.
0.6 × 250 = 150 mL, one tenth more than 60 per each tenth of the cup.
250.6 mL adds the decimal to the total instead of taking a fraction of it.

items.stem: A tablet contains 120 mg of medication, and 30% of that mass is the active drug. How many milligrams of active drug are in the tablet?
items.rationale: Change 30% to the decimal 0.30, then multiply: 0.30 × 120 mg = 36 mg of the drug.
distractor_rationales: 3.6 mg comes from using 0.03 instead of 0.30 when multiplying.
40 mg comes from rounding or guessing a quarter of the dose instead of computing.
Convert 30% to 0.30 and multiply: 0.30 × 120 mg = 36 mg.
360 mg comes from multiplying by 3, treating 30% as if it were 300%.

items.stem: A nutritional drink supplies 0.125 of a patient's daily protein requirement per serving. Written as a percent, this is closest to which value?
items.rationale: Multiply by 100 by shifting the decimal two places right: 0.125 becomes 12.5, so 0.125 = 12.5%.
distractor_rationales: 125% comes from moving the decimal point three places right instead of two.
1.25% comes from moving the decimal point only one place right.
0.125% leaves the decimal value unchanged and simply adds the percent sign.
Move the point two places right: 0.125 × 100 = 12.5, so 0.125 = 12.5%.

items.stem: Of the 180 medication doses scheduled on a unit this week, 45 were antibiotics. What percent of the doses were antibiotics?
items.rationale: Percent = part ÷ whole × 100 = 45 ÷ 180 × 100 = 0.25 × 100 = 25% of the scheduled doses.
distractor_rationales: 4% comes from inverting the ratio and computing 45 ÷ 1800 or a similar setup error.
40% comes from rounding 25% up, confusing it with a common benchmark fraction.
2.5% comes from dividing 180 by 45 and misplacing the decimal in the result.
Divide part by whole: 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25, and 0.25 = 25%.

llm_review.issues: Distractors are only moderately plausible; 40% and 4% do not clearly map to common calculation errors.

items.stem: A patient's weight decreased from 80 kg to 72 kg over one month. What was the percent decrease in the patient's weight?
items.rationale: Change = 80 − 72 = 8 kg. Percent decrease = 8 ÷ 80 = 0.10 = 10%, using the original weight as the base.
distractor_rationales: Percent decrease = change ÷ original = 8 ÷ 80 = 0.10 = 10%.
8% is the raw difference in kilograms written with a percent sign; the change must be divided by the original weight.
11.1% uses the new weight (72 kg) as the base instead of the original weight.
90% is the percent of the original weight that remains, not the percent decrease.

items.stem: A pharmacy used 25% of a vial of medication, leaving 300 mg in the vial. How many milligrams were in the vial originally?
items.rationale: If 25% was used, 75% remains, so 300 mg = 0.75 × original. Divide: 300 ÷ 0.75 = 400 mg originally in the vial.
distractor_rationales: 375 mg adds 25% of the remaining amount, but 300 mg is 75% of the original, not the whole.
The remaining 300 mg is 75% of the original, so 300 ÷ 0.75 = 400 mg.
450 mg comes from dividing by about 0.67, an error in handling the 75% portion.
325 mg simply adds the 25 to 300, mixing a percent with a plain count.

math_fractions.title: Fractions: simplify, add, subtract, multiply, divide
math_fractions.intro_markdown: Fractions name parts of a whole: the bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts make one whole, and the top number (numerator) tells how many parts you have. Four skills cover most exam questions. Simplify by dividing both numbers by their greatest common factor: 18/24 becomes 3/4 because 6 divides both 18 and 24. To add or subtract, first rewrite the fractions with a common denominator, then combine the numerators only: 1/4 + 1/6 equals 3/12 + 2/12, which is 5/12. To multiply, multiply straight across and simplify: 2/3 times 3/4 is 6/12, or 1/2. To divide, keep the first fraction, flip the second, and multiply: 1/2 divided by 1/8 is 1/2 times 8/1, which is 4. For mixed numbers like 2 1/2, convert to an improper fraction (5/2) before multiplying or dividing, and borrow from the whole number when a subtraction needs it.
key_points: Simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.
Add or subtract only after rewriting fractions with a common denominator.
Multiply straight across, then simplify; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing; borrow from the whole number when subtracting mixed numbers.

items.stem: Simplify the fraction 18/24 to lowest terms.
items.rationale: The greatest common factor of 18 and 24 is 6. Dividing numerator and denominator by 6 gives 3/4, and 3 and 4 share no common factor other than 1, so the fraction is fully simplified.
distractor_rationales: Correct: dividing 18 and 24 by the GCF 6 gives 3/4, which shares no factor other than 1.
Dividing by 9 (only 18 works) or guessing a common factor produced 2/3, which is not equivalent to 18/24.
Dividing by only 3 leaves 6/8, which can still be reduced to 3/4, so it is not fully simplified.
Dividing by only 2 leaves 9/12, which can still be reduced to 3/4, so it is not fully simplified.

items.stem: A patient receives 1/4 of a tablet in the morning and 1/6 of a tablet in the evening. What total fraction of a tablet does the patient receive per day?
items.rationale: The least common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12. Rewrite: 1/4 = 3/12 and 1/6 = 2/12. Adding numerators gives 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12 of a tablet.
distractor_rationales: Adding numerators and denominators (1+1 over 4+6 = 2/10) simplifies to 1/5, but denominators are never added.
Multiplying instead of adding gives 1/24; the operation here requires a common denominator.
Correct: the least common denominator is 12, so 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.
The LCD was found as 12, but 1/6 was rewritten as 4/12 (adding 6 to the denominator), giving 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12.

items.stem: An IV bag starts 5/6 full. By mid-shift, 1/3 of the bag has infused into the patient. What fraction of the bag remains?
items.rationale: Rewrite 1/3 as 2/6 using the common denominator 6. Then 5/6 - 2/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2 of the bag remaining.
distractor_rationales: Subtracting 1/6 instead of 1/3 (skipping the common-denominator step) gives 5/6 - 1/6 = 4/6.
The subtraction 3/6 is correct work but is not simplified to lowest terms.
This reverses the order of subtraction (2/6 - 5/6 treated as positive), yielding 2/3.
Correct: with the LCD of 6, 5/6 - 2/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2.

items.stem: A speech therapist prepares 2/3 cup of thickened juice, and the patient consumes 3/4 of it. How much juice did the patient actually drink?
items.rationale: Multiplying fractions means multiplying numerators (2 x 3 = 6) and denominators (3 x 4 = 12). The product 6/12 simplifies to 1/2 cup.
distractor_rationales: Adding the numerators and denominators gives 5/7, but denominators are never added when combining fractions.
Correct: multiplying straight across, 2 x 3 = 6 and 3 x 4 = 12, and 6/12 simplifies to 1/2.
Adding the numerators (2 + 3) over the product of the denominators (3 x 4) gives 5/12.
Cross-multiplying the numerators and denominators (2 x 4 and 3 x 3) gives 8/9, which is not how fractions are multiplied.

items.stem: A home-health aide starts with 3 1/2 oz of medicated ointment and uses 1 3/4 oz on a wound dressing. How much ointment is left in the tube?
items.rationale: Convert 3 1/2 to 3 2/4. Since 2/4 is less than 3/4, borrow 1 whole (4/4): 2 6/4 - 1 3/4 = 1 3/4, so 1 3/4 oz of ointment remains.
distractor_rationales: Subtracting the whole numbers (3 - 1 = 2) and the fraction parts in the wrong order (3/4 - 2/4 = 1/4) gives 2 1/4 oz; no borrowing was done.
The difference of the fraction parts, 2/4 - 3/4 = -1/4, was treated as 1/4 while also miscounting the whole numbers, giving 1 1/4 oz.
The 1/4 remaining fraction was left unsimplified from an incorrect borrow that used 3/4 as the borrowed amount.

items.stem: A dietary aide prepares 2 1/2 servings of low-sodium broth. Each serving contains 1 1/3 cups of broth. How many cups does the aide prepare in total?
items.rationale: Convert to improper fractions: 2 1/2 = 5/2 and 1 1/3 = 4/3. Multiply: 5/2 x 4/3 = 20/6 = 10/3 = 3 1/3 cups of broth.
distractor_rationales: Multiplying whole numbers separately from fractions (2 x 1 = 2 and 1/2 x 1/3 = 1/6) gives 2 1/6 cups; mixed numbers must be converted first.
Multiplying only the whole number 2 by 1 1/3 (and dropping the 1/2) gives 2 2/3 cups.
The two amounts were added (2 1/2 + 1 1/3 = 3 5/6) instead of multiplied.

items.stem: A container holds 5 1/4 cups of enteral feeding formula. Each patient feeding uses 3/4 cup. How many complete feedings does the container supply?
items.rationale: Convert 5 1/4 to 21/4, then multiply by the reciprocal of 3/4: 21/4 x 4/3 = 84/12 = 7. The container provides 7 complete feedings.
distractor_rationales: The amounts were added (5 1/4 + 3/4 = 6) instead of divided.
Multiplying by 3/4 instead of its reciprocal gives 21/4 x 3/4 = 63/16 = 3 15/16 feedings.
The first fraction was inverted instead of the second: 4/21 x 3/4 = 12/84 = 1/7 feeding.
Correct: 21/4 x 4/3 = 84/12 = 7 complete feedings.

items.stem: A hydration plan calls for 2/3 liter of oral fluid in the morning plus 1/6 liter at noon. The afternoon amount is 4/5 of the combined morning-and-noon total. How much fluid does the patient take in during the afternoon?
items.rationale: Work inside the parentheses first: 2/3 + 1/6 = 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6. Then multiply: 5/6 x 4/5 = 20/30, which simplifies to 2/3 L for the afternoon.
distractor_rationales: The sum 2/3 + 1/6 was incorrectly taken as exactly 1 liter, so the afternoon amount became 4/5 L.
The parentheses were ignored: this is only the sum 5/6, with the multiplication by 4/5 never applied.
The multiplication 2/3 x 4/5 = 8/15 was done first, then 1/6 was added, giving 7/10 L instead of following the parentheses.

math_ratios_proportions.title: Ratios and proportions, solving for x
math_ratios_proportions.intro_markdown: A ratio compares two quantities, and a proportion states that two ratios are equal. To solve for an unknown value x in a proportion, cross-multiply and then divide. For example, if an IV delivers 12 mL in 20 minutes, the amount delivered in 5 minutes follows from 12/20 = x/5. Cross-multiplying gives 20x = 60, so x = 3 mL. The same setup works for medication strength, staffing levels, and mixture problems. Always keep matching units in matching positions (mL with mL, minutes with minutes) before cross-multiplying. When simplifying a ratio, divide both parts by their greatest common factor, and write units next to your answer so the result stays meaningful in a clinical context.
key_points: A proportion sets two ratios equal; cross-multiply to clear the fractions, then divide to isolate x.
Match units across the proportion: same-unit quantities must occupy corresponding positions.
Simplify a ratio by dividing both terms by their greatest common factor.
Unit rates (per one tablet, per one mL, per one patient) make multi-step comparisons easier.
For dilution problems, the amount of pure drug stays constant; set up an equation based on that fixed quantity.

items.stem: A pharmacist mixes 18 mL of one liquid with 24 mL of another. What is this ratio in simplest form?
items.rationale: Both 18 and 24 divide by the GCF of 6, giving 18÷6 = 3 and 24÷6 = 4, so the simplified ratio is 3:4.
distractor_rationales: 18/24 reduces to 3/4 because both parts divide evenly by 6.
Reverses the order of the terms; 4:3 compares 24 to 18 instead of 18 to 24.
6:8 is a partial reduction (dividing by only 3) and is not fully simplified.
2:3 would come from dividing 18 by 9 but 24 by 8, using different divisors for each term.

items.stem: A bottle contains 240 mg of a medication divided evenly among 8 tablets. How many milligrams are in each tablet?
items.rationale: Unit rate = total amount ÷ number of units: 240 mg ÷ 8 tablets = 30 mg per tablet.
distractor_rationales: 32 mg would come from dividing by 7.5 rather than by the actual 8 tablets.
40 mg would come from dividing 240 by 6 tablets instead of 8.
240 mg ÷ 8 tablets = 30 mg per tablet, the unit rate.
20 mg would come from dividing 240 by 12 tablets instead of 8.

items.stem: An IV pump delivers 12 mL of fluid in 20 minutes. At the same rate, how much does it deliver in 5 minutes?
items.rationale: Equal rates give the proportion 12/20 = x/5. Cross-multiply: 20x = 60, so x = 3 mL delivered in 5 minutes.
distractor_rationales: 2 mL would come from dividing 12 by 5 instead of setting up a correct proportion.
Set the rates equal: 12/20 = x/5, so 20x = 60 and x = 3 mL at the same flow rate.
4 mL would come from using 60 as the product without finishing the division 60÷20.
5 mL mistakenly copies the denominator instead of solving for the unknown amount.

items.stem: A liquid medication contains 250 mg of drug in every 5 mL. How many milligrams of the drug are in a 12 mL dose?
items.rationale: 250/5 = x/12, so 5x = 3000 and x = 600 mg. Equivalently, 50 mg/mL × 12 mL = 600 mg.
distractor_rationales: 625 mg would come from multiplying 250 by 25 rather than by the correct per-mL factor of 50.
60 mg would come from multiplying 5 mL by 12 and keeping the wrong units in the proportion.
First find the unit strength: 250 mg ÷ 5 mL = 50 mg/mL; then 50 × 12 mL = 600 mg.
500 mg would come from doubling 250 mg instead of scaling by the full 12/5 factor.

items.stem: Four tablets of a supplement contain 1200 mg of calcium. At the same strength, how many milligrams are in 6 tablets?
items.rationale: The proportion 1200/4 = x/6 gives 4x = 7200, so x = 1800 mg across 6 tablets.
